title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 What is a point pattern?
stelfi fits Hawkes processes, log-Gaussian Cox processes (LGCPs), and spatiotemporal self-exciting models to point pattern data. All models are fitted by maximum likelihood using Template Model Builder (TMB, Kristensen et al. (2016)), which makes fitting fast even for fairly large datasets. Where a model includes a spatial random field, the field is assumed to be Gaussian, it is built using the stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) approach of Lindgren, Rue, and Lindström (2011), and it is integrated out of the likelihood using the Laplace approximation.
This book is written for people who have point pattern data of their own and want to know (1) which stelfi model suits their data, (2) what shape the data need to be in, (3) how to fit and interpret the model, and (4) how to check whether the model is any good. The emphasis is on using the models rather than on the theory behind them.
A point pattern is a record of when and/or where events happened. Examples are the times of retweets of a tweet, the locations of sasquatch sightings, or the times, locations, and magnitudes of earthquakes. The thing being modelled is the intensity, the expected rate of events per unit time (or per unit area, or per unit area per unit time). A high intensity means events are likely, a low intensity means events are unlikely.
The models in stelfi differ in why the intensity varies:

title: 1  Introduction
text:
In a Hawkes process events cause more events. Each event temporarily increases the chance of another event occurring soon afterwards (self-excitement). Think of aftershocks following an earthquake or retweets following a tweet.
In a log-Gaussian Cox process the intensity varies smoothly over space (and time) because of some underlying, unobserved, environment. Events do not cause other events, they are just more common in some places than others. Think of where species are found or where crimes tend to occur.
A spatiotemporal self-exciting model combines the two: there is a background intensity over space and events trigger further events nearby in both space and time.

section: 1.3 How the model chapters are organised
text:
1.3 How the model chapters are organised
Each of the model fitting chapters (Chapter 2 to Chapter 8, other than Chapter 5 on meshes) follows the same structure:

The model and your data: a short description of the model, what the parameters mean, and what your data need to look like (including common problems and limitations).
A simulated example: data are simulated from the model with known parameter values. The model is then fitted using stelfi and, where one exists, a competing R package, and the estimates from both are compared with each other and with the truth. The code used to simulate the data is shown, so that every chapter is fully reproducible, and so that you can change the parameter values (or the amount of data) and see how well the model is estimated.
An applied example: the model is fitted to one of the datasets that come with stelfi (see Chapter 10) and the estimates are interpreted.
Goodness-of-fit: some procedures to check whether the fitted model adequately describes the data.

The chapters build on one another: the univariate Hawkes chapter (Chapter 2) introduces ideas used in all of the Hawkes-type chapters, and the chapter on meshes (Chapter 5) and the spatial LGCP chapter (Chapter 6) introduce ideas used in all of the spatial chapters. If you are new to these models, start there.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.4 A typical stelfi workflow
Whatever the model, using stelfi involves the same steps:

Prepare the data. Times must be numeric (e.g., days since the first event) and sorted. Locations must be in a projected (planar) coordinate system, such as UTM, ideally in sensible units (e.g., km).
For spatial models, define the study region and build a mesh. The study region is an sf polygon and the mesh is a triangulation of it built with fmesher::fm_mesh_2d() (see Chapter 5).
Choose starting values for the parameters and fit the model with one of the fit_*() functions.
Extract the estimates using get_coefs() (and, for spatial models, the estimated random field using get_fields()).
Visualise the fitted model using show_hawkes(), show_multivariate_hawkes(), show_field() or show_lambda().
Check the fit using show_hawkes_GOF() (temporal models) or simulation-based checks (spatial models).

title: 2  Univariate Hawkes process
text:
2.1 The model and your data
A univariate Hawkes process (Hawkes (1971)) is a model for event times where the occurrence of an event temporarily increases the chance of further events. It is described by its conditional intensity, the expected rate of events at time \(t\) given everything that has happened before \(t\),
\[\lambda(t) = \mu + \alpha \sum_{i:\tau_i<t}\text{exp}(-\beta (t-\tau_i)), \tag{2.1}\]
where \(\tau_1, \tau_2, ...\) are the event times. There are three parameters:
Two derived quantities are usually of most interest:
Plotted below is the conditional intensity of a Hawkes process with \(\mu = 0.5\), \(\alpha = 1\), and \(\beta = 1.5\). The events are shown by the vertical dashes along the x-axis. The intensity jumps by \(\alpha\) each time an event occurs and decays exponentially back towards \(\mu\) if no event occurs.
Code for this figure
mu <- 0.5; alpha <- 1; beta <- 1.5
tim <- sim_hawkes(mu = mu, alpha = alpha, beta = beta, n = 15)
p <- seq(min(tim), max(tim), length.out = 1000)
lamda <- stelfi:::hawkes_intensity(mu = mu, alpha = alpha, beta = beta, times = tim, p = p)
ggplot(data.frame(x = p, y = lamda), aes(x = x, y = y)) +
    xlab("") + ylab(expression(lambda(t))) +
    geom_line() + theme_minimal() +
    geom_point(data = data.frame(x = tim, y = 0.2), pch = "|", size = 5) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = c("t = 0","t = T"),
                       breaks = seq(min(p), max(p), length.out = 2))

title: 2  Univariate Hawkes process
text:
\(\mu\), the background rate: the rate at which “spontaneous” events occur, i.e., events not triggered by any earlier event;
\(\alpha\), the jump in the intensity immediately after each event; and
\(\beta\), the decay rate: how quickly the extra intensity caused by an event dies away. \(1/\beta\) is roughly how long (in the units of your times) an event continues to have an influence.



the branching ratio \(\alpha/\beta\), the expected number of events directly triggered by any one event. This must be less than 1 (otherwise the process explodes), and stelfi enforces \(\alpha \leq \beta\); and
the expected number of background events over the observation period \([0, T]\), which is \(\mu T\). The proportion of events that are background events is roughly \(1 - \alpha/\beta\).




2.1.1 What your data need to look like
fit_hawkes() requires a single numeric vector of event times. Some things to be aware of:

Times must be numeric, sorted, and start near zero. Dates or date-times (e.g., POSIXct) need to be converted to a number, for example with as.numeric(difftime(x, min(x), units = "days")). The units you choose (seconds, minutes, days, …) set the units of the parameters: \(\mu\) is then events per day (say) and \(1/\beta\) is in days. Choose units that make the numbers neither tiny nor huge.
No two events can have exactly the same time. stelfi will stop with an error if they do. Ties are very common when times are recorded to the nearest day or minute. You can either drop duplicates (e.g., unique(times)), which throws away information, or add a small random amount to each time (“jittering”) that is less than the recording resolution, e.g., a random number of seconds within the recorded minute (see Section 3.3). If a large proportion of your events are tied the recording resolution is too coarse relative to the speed of the self-excitement and a Hawkes model may not be appropriate.
The observation period is assumed to be from \(t = 0\) to the last event. If you watched for events for longer than this, the background rate will be slightly overestimated. Starting the times at the first event (rather than the true start of observation) has a similar small effect.
The background rate is assumed to be constant. If events are more common at certain times of day or year for reasons unrelated to self-excitement, this will be mistaken for self-excitement. See Section 2.5 for a model with a time-varying background.
Self-excitement is assumed to decay exponentially. For some processes (e.g., earthquake aftershocks) the influence of an event decays much more slowly than this, which the goodness-of-fit checks in Section 2.4 will usually reveal.
All events are assumed to be of the same type and of the same importance. See Chapter 3 if events differ in how much they trigger, and Chapter 4 if there are different types of event.

As a rough guide you need at least a hundred or so events to estimate the three parameters with any precision.

title: 2  Univariate Hawkes process
text:
2.2 A simulated example
Data were simulated from a Hawkes process with \(\mu = 1.3\), \(\alpha = 0.4\), and \(\beta = 1.5\) over \(t \in [0, 500]\) (so the true branching ratio is \(\alpha/\beta =\) 0.267) using sim_hawkes(). Here n is the end of the observation period (not the number of events), and seed sets the random number seed so that the same data are simulated every time.

times <- sim_hawkes(mu = 1.3, alpha = 0.4, beta = 1.5, n = 500, seed = 123)

The data are simply a sorted numeric vector of 885 event times:

head(times)

[1] 0.9586637 1.1416407 1.2148232 2.6856813 2.7312091 3.4665714



2.2.1 Fitting the model using stelfi
To fit a univariate Hawkes model in stelfi use fit_hawkes() with

times, the vector of event times, and
parameters, a named vector of starting values for \(\mu\) (mu), \(\alpha\) (alpha), and \(\beta\) (beta).

The estimates (and standard errors) are returned by get_coefs().

sv <- c(mu = 1, alpha = 0.5, beta = 2)
fit <- fit_hawkes(times = times, parameters = sv)
stelfi <- get_coefs(fit)
stelfi

       Estimate Std. Error
mu    1.3999339  0.1125087
alpha 0.3734267  0.1207302
beta  1.7719772  0.7488404




2.2.2 Comparison with emhawkes and hawkesbow
The same model can be fitted using the emhawkes (Lee (2023)) and hawkesbow (Cheysson (2021)) packages. Note that emhawkes requires the times between events rather than the event times (and here final_hessian = "stable" is used, as the default numerical Hessian can fail to give standard errors).

## emhawkes
library(emhawkes)
h <- new("hspec", mu = sv[1], alpha = sv[2], beta = sv[3])
inter <- c(0, diff(times))
fit_em <- hfit(object = h, inter_arrival = inter, final_hessian = "stable")
em <- summary(fit_em)$estimate
em

        Estimate Std. error   t value      Pr(> t)
mu1    1.4003963  0.1131465 12.376845 3.487871e-35
alpha1 0.3700542  0.1195182  3.096216 1.960078e-03
beta1  1.7539005  0.7394766  2.371813 1.770103e-02

## hawkesbow
library(hawkesbow)
fit_bow <- mle(events = times, kern = "Exponential", end = max(times))
## standard errors from the Hessian
bow <- cbind(Estimate = fit_bow$par,
             "Std. error" = -fit_bow$model$ddloglik(times, max(times)) |>
                 solve() |> diag() |> sqrt())

title: 2  Univariate Hawkes process
section: 2.3 An applied example: retweets of a viral tweet
text:
2.3 An applied example: retweets of a viral tweet
A NIWA scientist found a working USB stick in the scat of a leopard seal and tweeted about it in the hope of finding its owner. The times of the retweets are available in stelfi as retweets_niwa (see Chapter 10). Retweets are a natural candidate for a Hawkes process: each retweet exposes the tweet to more people, who may then retweet it themselves.

data(retweets_niwa, package = "stelfi")
head(retweets_niwa)

[1] "2019-02-07 06:50:08 UTC" "2019-02-07 06:50:08 UTC"
[3] "2019-02-07 06:49:22 UTC" "2019-02-07 06:48:48 UTC"
[5] "2019-02-07 06:47:52 UTC" "2019-02-07 06:47:42 UTC"


The data are date-times (POSIXct). They are converted to minutes since the first retweet. Retweets are recorded to the nearest second, and a number of retweets share the same second; here duplicate times are simply dropped using unique() (see Section 2.1.1 for an alternative).

times <- unique(sort(as.numeric(difftime(retweets_niwa, min(retweets_niwa), units = "mins"))))
length(retweets_niwa) - length(times) ## number of dropped duplicates

[1] 118


The histogram below shows the number of retweets per hour from the original tweet to the time (just over two days later) that the owner of the USB stick came forward.


Code for this figure
start <- lubridate::ymd_hms("2019-02-05 02:27:07")
end <- lubridate::ymd_hms("2019-02-07 06:50:08")
hist(retweets_niwa, breaks = "hours", axes = FALSE,
     xlab = "", ylab = "", main = "", col = "grey", border = "grey", freq = TRUE)
axis(2, at = c(0, 250))
mtext(2, line = 0, text = "Number of retweets per hour", cex = 0.8)
mtext(1, line = 1, at = c(start, end), text = c("NIWA \n tweeted", "USB owner \n found"), cex = 0.9)









To fit the model choose some starting values and supply these, along with the numeric times, to fit_hawkes().

sv <- c(mu = 9, alpha = 3, beta = 10)
fit <- fit_hawkes(times = times, parameters = sv)
pars <- get_coefs(fit)
pars

        Estimate  Std. Error
mu    0.06328099 0.017783908
alpha 0.07596531 0.007777899
beta  0.07911346 0.008109789


From the estimates above (time is in minutes):

the expected number of background retweets is \(\hat{\mu}T =\) 0.063 \(\times\) 3143 \(=\) 198.9, so only around 199 of the 4772 retweets were “spontaneous” and the remainder were triggered by earlier retweets;
the branching ratio is \(\hat{\alpha}/\hat{\beta}\) = 0.96, i.e., each retweet directly triggers 0.96 further retweets on average; and
\(1/\hat{\beta}\) = 12.64 minutes, so the influence of a retweet largely dies away after around 13 minutes.

The show_hawkes() function plots the estimated conditional intensity (top) and the data (bottom).

show_hawkes(fit, type = "both")

title: 2  Univariate Hawkes process
text:
2.4 Goodness-of-fit

2.4.1 The idea
The compensator \(\Lambda(t) = \int_0^{t} \lambda(s) ds\) is the expected number of events up to time \(t\) under the fitted model. The random time change theorem (Daley, Vere-Jones, et al. (2003)) says that if the model is correct, then the transformed times \(\Lambda(\tau_1), \Lambda(\tau_2), ...\) behave like a homogeneous Poisson process with rate 1. Equivalently, the compensator differences \(\Lambda(\tau_i) - \Lambda(\tau_{i-1})\) should be independent draws from an \(\text{Exp}(1)\) distribution. This gives two standard checks:

a Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test of whether the compensator differences follow an \(\text{Exp}(1)\) distribution; and
a Ljung-Box test of whether consecutive compensator differences are correlated (they should not be).

Small p-values indicate that the model does not describe the data well. With large datasets these tests will detect even small departures from the model, so the accompanying plots are often more useful than the p-values.


2.4.2 What a good fit looks like
The compensator differences can be extracted using compensator_differences() and tested directly. For the model fitted to the simulated data in Section 2.2 (where the model is correct):

## the same simulated data as in the simulated example (same parameters and seed)
times_sim <- sim_hawkes(mu = 1.3, alpha = 0.4, beta = 1.5, n = 500, seed = 123)
fit_sim <- fit_hawkes(times = times_sim, parameters = c(mu = 1, alpha = 0.5, beta = 2))


compensator <- compensator_differences(fit_sim)
stats::ks.test(compensator, "pexp")


    Asymptotic one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

data:  compensator
D = 0.013855, p-value = 0.9958
alternative hypothesis: two-sided

stats::Box.test(compensator, type = "Ljung")


    Box-Ljung test

data:  compensator
X-squared = 0.66583, df = 1, p-value = 0.4145


There is no evidence against the compensator differences being independent \(\text{Exp}(1)\) draws. The function show_hawkes_GOF() carries out both tests and draws four diagnostic plots:

top left, the compensator (expected number of events) and the observed cumulative number of events against time, these should lie close to one another;
top right, a QQ plot of the compensator differences against the \(\text{Exp}(1)\) distribution, the points should lie on the line;
bottom left, a histogram of the compensator differences, which should look like an \(\text{Exp}(1)\) distribution; and
bottom right, consecutive compensator differences (on the probability scale) plotted against each other, which should show no pattern.


show_hawkes_GOF(fit_sim)


    Asymptotic one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

data:  interarrivals
D = 0.013855, p-value = 0.9958
alternative hypothesis: two-sided


    Box-Ljung test

data:  interarrivals
X-squared = 0.66583, df = 1, p-value = 0.4145











2.4.3 The retweet model

show_hawkes_GOF(fit)


    Asymptotic one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

data:  interarrivals
D = 0.031122, p-value = 0.0001937
alternative hypothesis: two-sided


    Box-Ljung test

data:  interarrivals
X-squared = 3.3923, df = 1, p-value = 0.0655









The compensator follows the observed number of retweets closely (top left), so the model captures the overall rise and fall in retweeting, and the Ljung-Box test gives little evidence of correlation between consecutive compensator differences. The KS test, however, gives a small p-value. With nearly 5000 events the test is very sensitive, and the QQ plot shows the model is broadly adequate: the main departure is that there are fewer very short gaps between retweets than the model expects. This is at least partly an artefact of the data, since times are recorded to the nearest second and tied retweets were dropped (Section 2.1.1), so very short gaps cannot appear in the data. Note too that the estimated branching ratio is close to 1, which is typical of “viral” behaviour but means the background and self-excitement are hard to separate. Possible next steps are jittering the tied times rather than dropping them, a time-varying background (Section 2.5), or including information on the retweeter, such as their number of followers, as a mark (Chapter 3).

title: 2  Univariate Hawkes process
text:
2.5 Extension: a time-varying background rate
In some applications the background rate itself changes over time, for example with the time of day or the season. Ignoring this can make it look as though there is self-excitement when really events are just more common at certain times. A Hawkes process with a time-varying background replaces \(\mu\) in Equation 2.1 with a function \(\mu(t)\). This model is fitted in stelfi using fit_hawkes_cbf() (custom background function).
Data were simulated (using hawkesbow, Cheysson (2021)) over 1000 days from a Hawkes process with a yearly cycle in the background, \(\mu(t) = A + B\,\text{sin}(\frac{2 \pi t}{365.25})\), with \(A = 1\) and \(B = 0.5\), and self-excitement parameters \(\alpha = 1\) and \(\beta = 2\). hawkesbow::hawkes() parameterises the exponential kernel by the branching ratio (repr \(= \alpha/\beta\)) and the decay rate (rate \(= \beta\)), and M is an upper bound on the background function, used to simulate the background events by thinning.

mut <- function(t) 1 + 0.5 * sin((2 * pi * t) / 365.25) ## the background rate mu(t)
set.seed(1)
times <- hawkesbow::hawkes(1000, fun = mut, M = 1.5, repr = 0.5, family = "exp", rate = 2)$p

As before the data are a sorted vector of 2056 event times.
To fit this model you need to supply both \(\mu(t)\) (background) and its integral \(\int_0^t \mu(s) ds\) (background_integral) as functions of a vector of parameters and time. To ensure \(\mu(t) > 0\) the parameters are transformed: \(A = e^{x}\) and \(B = \text{logit}^{-1}(y) A\), so that \(0 < B < A\).

background <- function(params, t) {
    A <- exp(params[[1]])
    B <- stats::plogis(params[[2]]) * A
    A + B * sin((2 * pi * t) / 365.25)
}
background_integral <- function(params, x) {
    A <- exp(params[[1]])
    B <- stats::plogis(params[[2]]) * A
    (A * x) - B * cos((2 * pi * x) / 365.25)
}

These are passed to fit_hawkes_cbf() along with the times, starting values for \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) (parameters), and starting values for the background parameters (background_parameters).

fit <- fit_hawkes_cbf(times = times, parameters = list(alpha = 0.5, beta = 1.5),
                      background = background, background_integral = background_integral,
                      background_parameters = list(1, 1))

title: 3  Marked Hawkes process
text:
3.1 The model and your data
In the univariate Hawkes process (Chapter 2) every event triggers further events in exactly the same way. Often, though, some events are more “important” than others: a large earthquake triggers more aftershocks than a small one, and a tweet from an account with many followers is retweeted more than one from an account with few. If each event has a numeric value (a mark) that describes its importance, a marked Hawkes process lets the size of the jump in intensity after an event depend on that mark. In stelfi the conditional intensity is
\[\lambda(t) = \mu + \alpha \sum_{i:\tau_i<t}m(\tau_i)\,\text{exp}(-\beta (t-\tau_i)), \tag{3.1}\]
where \(m(\tau_i)\) is the mark of the event at time \(\tau_i\). The only difference to Equation 2.1 is that the jump after event \(i\) is \(\alpha m(\tau_i)\) rather than \(\alpha\), so an event with mark 2 has twice the effect of an event with mark 1. The parameters \(\mu\), \(\alpha\), and \(\beta\) are interpreted as in Chapter 2, except that the expected number of events triggered by an event with mark \(m\) is \(\alpha m / \beta\), and the average branching ratio is \(\alpha \bar{m} / \beta\), where \(\bar{m}\) is the average mark. stelfi constrains the average branching ratio to be less than 1.

title: 3  Marked Hawkes process
text:
3.1.1 What your data need to look like
You need two numeric vectors of the same length: the event times (exactly as in Section 2.1.1, sorted with no ties) and the marks, where marks[i] belongs to times[i]. In addition:

Marks must be non-negative, and an event with a mark of 0 triggers nothing.
The scale of the marks matters. Because the mark multiplies the jump, doubling all of the marks halves \(\alpha\), and adding a constant to all of the marks changes the model. You will usually want to transform your raw measurement into a mark that is proportional to how much you believe an event triggers. For example, in seismology the number of aftershocks is believed to grow exponentially with magnitude, so \(\text{exp}(\text{magnitude} - c)\) is a more natural mark than the magnitude itself (see Section 3.3). Different transformations can be compared using the likelihood (e.g., AIC).
The marks are treated as known. The model describes how marks affect future events but does not model the marks themselves (e.g., it does not predict the magnitude of the next earthquake). Missing marks need to be dealt with before fitting.
Marks only affect triggering, not the background. If the marks are also related to the background rate (e.g., larger events are rarer) this is not captured.

title: 3  Marked Hawkes process
text:
3.2 A simulated example
Data were simulated (using emhawkes, Lee (2023)) from a marked Hawkes process with \(\mu = 0.5\), \(\alpha = 0.3\), and \(\beta = 1.5\), where each event’s mark is equally likely to be 1, 2, 3, or 4. So an event with mark 4 increases the intensity by \(4 \times 0.3 = 1.2\), whereas an event with mark 1 increases it by only \(0.3\). In emhawkes the marks are generated by the function rmark, and the extra jump in the intensity caused by an event’s mark is given by the function impact: here \(0.3 \times (\text{mark} - 1)\), so that the total jump is \(0.3 \times \text{mark}\).

library(emhawkes)
fn_mark <- function(...) sample(1:4, 1) ## each mark is equally likely to be 1, 2, 3, or 4
impact <- function(param = c(eta1 = 0.3), alpha, n, mark, ...) {
    matrix(param["eta1"] * (mark[n] - 1), nrow = 1)
}
h_sim <- new("hspec", mu = 0.5, alpha = 0.3, beta = 1.5, rmark = fn_mark, impact = impact)
set.seed(1)
res <- hsim(h_sim, size = 1000, lambda_component0 = matrix(0.5))
## drop the dummy event at t = 0 that emhawkes adds
sim <- data.frame(times = res$arrival[-1], marks = res$mark[-1])

3.4 Goodness-of-fit
The goodness-of-fit procedures for the marked model are exactly those described in Section 2.4: the compensator now includes the marks, but show_hawkes_GOF() takes care of this. For the simulated example (where the model is correct) there is no evidence of lack of fit:

alternative hypothesis: two-sided

data:  interarrivals

For both models the tests give very small p-values, and the plots show where the models fall short. Before the first large earthquake (around day 230) the compensator lies above the observed number of earthquakes, so the background rate is overestimated in this quiet period, while after each large earthquake the compensator lags below the observed count, so the models underpredict the number of aftershocks. The cluster of points in the bottom left corner of the consecutive compensator differences plot shows that short gaps tend to be followed by short gaps, which is the correlation picked up by the Ljung-Box test. Including the magnitudes improves the likelihood considerably (see the AIC above), but the diagnostic plots for the two models look similar, and neither model is fully adequate.
This is a well known feature of earthquake data: aftershock activity decays like a power law in time (the Omori-Utsu law) rather than exponentially, so an exponential kernel cannot capture both the very intense activity immediately after a large earthquake and the long tail of aftershocks that follows. Models designed specifically for earthquakes (e.g., the ETAS model) use a power law kernel. The background rate is also unlikely to be constant over the whole period. The marked Hawkes model is still useful, for example for quantifying how much more a large earthquake triggers than a small one, but its estimates should be interpreted with these limitations in mind.

title: 4  Multivariate Hawkes process
text:
4.1 The model and your data
Often events come in different types, or streams, and events of one type can trigger events of another. For example, large earthquakes trigger small ones, attacks by one group might provoke attacks by another, and buy orders on a stock exchange can trigger sell orders. A multivariate Hawkes process extends the univariate Hawkes process (Chapter 2) so that each stream has its own intensity, and every event can increase the intensity of every stream. In stelfi the conditional intensity of stream \(j\) (\(j = 1, ..., N\)) is
\[\lambda_j(t) = \mu_j + \sum_{k = 1}^N \alpha_{jk} \sum_{i:\tau_i<t,\ s_i = k} \text{exp}(-\beta_j (t-\tau_i)), \tag{4.1}\]
where \(s_i\) is the stream of the event at time \(\tau_i\). The parameters are
The expected number of stream \(j\) events directly triggered by a single stream \(k\) event is \(\alpha_{jk}/\beta_j\). stelfi constrains each of these to be at most 1 (i.e., \(\alpha_{jk} \leq \beta_j\)).
Plotted below are the conditional intensities of a bivariate (two stream) Hawkes process with \(\boldsymbol{\mu} = (0.5, 0.9)\), \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}\) = \(\begin{bmatrix}0.2&0.1 \\0.6&0.5 \\\end{bmatrix}\), and \(\boldsymbol{\beta} = (0.7, 0.9)\). Events are shown by the vertical dashes along the x-axis. An event in either stream increases the intensity of both streams, but an event in stream 1 has a much bigger effect on stream 2 (\(\alpha_{21} = 0.6\)) than an event in stream 2 has on stream 1 (\(\alpha_{12} = 0.1\)).
Code for this figure
mu <- c(0.5, 0.9)
alpha <- matrix(c(0.2, 0.1 ,0.6, 0.5), byrow = TRUE, nrow = 2)
beta <- c(0.7, 0.9)
set.seed(1)
tmp <- hawkes::simulateHawkes(mu, alpha, beta, 10)
data <- data.frame(times = unlist(tmp), stream = rep(c("Stream 1", "Stream 2"), times = lengths(tmp)))
data <- data[order(data$times), ]
dat_2 <- data.frame(x = seq(min(data$times), max(data$times), length.out = 500))
tst <- stelfi:::multi_hawkes_intensity(times = data$times, alpha = alpha, mu = mu, beta = beta,
                                       p = dat_2$x, stream = data$stream)
dat_2$`Stream 1` <- tst[[1]]
dat_2$`Stream 2` <- tst[[2]]
data_2 <- tidyr::pivot_longer(dat_2, cols = 2:3, names_to = "stream")
ggplot(data_2, aes(x = x, y = value, col = stream, group = stream)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
    geom_point(data = data, aes(x = times, y = 0, col = stream, group = stream),
               pch = "|", size = 5) +
    theme_classic(base_size = 10) + ylab(expression(lambda[j]~"(t)")) + xlab("") +
    theme(legend.position = "top", legend.title = element_blank()) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("black", "grey")) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = c("t = 0","t = T"),
                       breaks = seq(min(data$times), max(data$times), length.out = 2))

title: 4  Multivariate Hawkes process
text:
\(\mu_j\), the background rate of stream \(j\);
\(\alpha_{jk}\), the jump in the intensity of stream \(j\) caused by an event in stream \(k\). These form an \(N \times N\) matrix \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}\): the diagonal elements (\(\alpha_{jj}\)) describe self-excitation (events triggering events of the same type) and the off-diagonal elements describe cross-excitation (events of one type triggering events of another type); and
\(\beta_j\), the rate at which excitement of stream \(j\) decays, i.e., how quickly the intensity of stream \(j\) returns to its background rate after an event in any stream.





4.1.1 What your data need to look like
fit_mhawkes() needs two vectors of the same length:

times, the event times of all streams combined, sorted in ascending order with no ties (see Section 2.1.1; ties between streams are not allowed either); and
stream, a character vector giving the stream of each event, so stream[i] is the type of the event at times[i].

In addition:

Streams are ordered alphabetically. Parameters for “stream 1” refer to the first stream name in alphabetical order. Choose stream names so that this order is the one you want (e.g., "A_small" and "B_large").
The number of parameters grows quickly. With \(N\) streams there are \(N + N^2 + N\) parameters (8 for two streams, 15 for three). Each stream needs a reasonable number of events, and in particular there need to be enough events in each stream to estimate the cross-excitation parameters. Two or three streams is usually plenty.
Every event must belong to exactly one stream. If your event types overlap, or the type is unknown for some events, these need to be dealt with before fitting.
The limitations of the univariate model apply to each stream: constant background rates, exponential decay, and an observation period from \(0\) to the last event.

text:
4.2 A simulated example
Data were simulated (using the hawkes package, Zaatour (2014)) from a bivariate Hawkes process with the parameters given above over the time period \(t \in [0, 500]\). hawkes::simulateHawkes() returns a list with the event times of each stream, which are combined into a single data frame with one row per event, sorted by time.

mu <- c(0.5, 0.9)
alpha <- matrix(c(0.2, 0.1 ,0.6, 0.5), byrow = TRUE, nrow = 2)
beta <- c(0.7, 0.9)
set.seed(1)
sim <- hawkes::simulateHawkes(mu, alpha, beta, 500)
data <- data.frame(times = unlist(sim), stream = rep(c("Stream 1", "Stream 2"), times = lengths(sim)))
data <- data[order(data$times), ]

Because there are many parameters it is a good idea to ask the optimiser (optim()) to use the "BFGS" method, which uses the gradient that TMB calculates, rather than the default (Nelder-Mead), which can stop before reaching the maximum.

4.2.2 Comparison with the hawkes package
The hawkes package (Zaatour (2014)) does not have a fitting function, but it does provide the negative log-likelihood (likelihoodHawkes()), which can be minimised using optim(). The parameters are estimated on the log scale (to keep them positive) and the standard errors are obtained from the Hessian using the delta method.

nll <- function(p) {
    hawkes::likelihoodHawkes(lambda0 = exp(p[1:2]),
                             alpha = matrix(exp(p[3:6]), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE),
                             beta = exp(p[7:8]), history = sim)
}

opt <- optim(start, nll, method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE)
est <- exp(opt$par)

## order: mu_1, mu_2, alpha_11, alpha_12, alpha_21, alpha_22, beta_1, beta_2

4.3 An applied example: large and small earthquakes
In Section 3.3 the magnitude of each Canterbury earthquake was used as a mark. An alternative is to split the earthquakes into two streams, small (magnitude 3 to 4) and large (magnitude 4 and above), and ask how much each type triggers the other. The data are prepared exactly as before (times in days, jittered to remove ties).

data(nz_earthquakes, package = "stelfi")
eq <- data.frame(time = nz_earthquakes$origintime, magnitude = nz_earthquakes$magnitude)
eq$days <- as.numeric(difftime(eq$time, min(eq$time), units = "days"))
set.seed(1)
eq$days <- eq$days + runif(nrow(eq), 0, 1 / (24 * 60))
eq <- eq[order(eq$days), ]
eq$days <- eq$days - eq$days[1]
## streams (alphabetical order: "M3-4" is stream 1, "M4+" is stream 2)
eq$size <- ifelse(eq$magnitude >= 4, "M4+", "M3-4")
table(eq$size)


M3-4  M4+ 
3445  379 



sv <- list(mu = c(0.3, 0.05),
           alpha = matrix(c(1, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5), nrow = 2),
           beta = c(2, 2))
fit_eq <- fit_mhawkes(times = eq$days, stream = eq$size, parameters = sv, method = "BFGS")
pars_eq <- get_coefs(fit_eq)
pars_eq

            Estimate Std. Error
mu_1      0.25435100 0.01649999
mu_2      0.06004952 0.00622599
alpha_11  1.97197679 0.11827898
alpha_21  1.58893270 0.26960421

## estimated parameters as a vector mu, a matrix alpha, and a vector beta
mhawkes_pars <- function(fit) {
    cf <- get_coefs(fit)[, 1]
    N <- length(table(fit$env$data$stream))
    list(mu = cf[1:N],
         alpha = matrix(cf[(N + 1):(N + N^2)], nrow = N), ## column-major order
         beta = cf[(N + N^2 + 1):(2 * N + N^2)])
}



Code
pe <- mhawkes_pars(fit_eq)
br <- sweep(pe$alpha, 1, pe$beta, "/")


Here stream 1 is small earthquakes and stream 2 is large earthquakes. It is easiest to interpret the estimates as the expected number of events of each type directly triggered by one event, \(\alpha_{jk}/\beta_j\):

pe <- mhawkes_pars(fit_eq)
branching <- sweep(pe$alpha, 1, pe$beta, "/") ## alpha_jk / beta_j
dimnames(branching) <- list(triggered = c("small", "large"), trigger = c("small", "large"))
round(branching, 3)

         trigger
triggered small large
    small 0.737 1.000
    large 0.025 0.487



A small earthquake triggers on average 0.74 further small earthquakes and only 0.025 large ones.
A large earthquake triggers on average 1 small earthquake(s) (see the note below) and 0.49 large ones.
After an earthquake, the rate of large earthquakes returns to its background level very quickly (\(1/\hat{\beta}_2 =\) 23 minutes), whereas the rate of small earthquakes stays raised for longer (\(1/\hat{\beta}_1 =\) 9 hours).

Notice that the estimate of \(\alpha_{12}/\beta_1\) (small earthquakes triggered by a large one) is 1, the maximum allowed by stelfi. In reality large earthquakes trigger many more than one aftershock each, so this constraint is limiting the model here, and the estimate should be read as “at least one”. The marked model (Section 3.3), where the effect of an earthquake grows continuously with its magnitude, does not have this limitation, and is probably a more natural model for these data.

title: 4  Multivariate Hawkes process
text:
4.4 Goodness-of-fit
The ideas of Section 2.4 apply to each stream separately: if the model is correct then, for each stream \(j\), the compensator \(\Lambda_j(t) = \int_0^t \lambda_j(s) ds\) evaluated at the times of the stream \(j\) events transforms them into a unit rate Poisson process, so the differences between consecutive values should be \(\text{Exp}(1)\). Note that \(\lambda_j(t)\) depends on the events in all streams. For Equation 4.1 the compensator is
\[\Lambda_j(t) = \mu_j t + \sum_{k=1}^N \frac{\alpha_{jk}}{\beta_j} \sum_{i:\tau_i < t,\ s_i = k} \left(1 - \text{exp}(-\beta_j (t - \tau_i))\right).\]
show_hawkes_GOF() does not (yet) work for multivariate models, but the compensator differences are easily calculated with the function below (which uses the helper mhawkes_pars() defined in Section 4.3), and the tests from Section 2.4 applied to each stream.

mhawkes_compensator_differences <- function(fit) {
    times <- fit$env$data$times
    stream <- fit$env$data$stream
    pars <- mhawkes_pars(fit)
    s <- as.integer(factor(stream))
    out <- lapply(seq_along(pars$mu), function(j) {
        comp <- sapply(times[s == j], function(t) {
            prev <- times < t
            pars$mu[j] * t + sum(pars$alpha[j, s[prev]] / pars$beta[j] *
                                 (1 - exp(-pars$beta[j] * (t - times[prev]))))
        })
        diff(c(0, comp))
    })
    names(out) <- sort(unique(stream))
    out
}

For the simulated example (where the model is correct) there is no evidence of lack of fit in either stream:

cd <- mhawkes_compensator_differences(fit)
sapply(cd, function(x) c(KS = ks.test(x, "pexp")$p.value,
                         Ljung_Box = Box.test(x, type = "Ljung")$p.value))

           Stream 1  Stream 2
KS        0.8882235 0.5665953
Ljung_Box 0.1629018 0.1751817


For the earthquake model:

cd_eq <- mhawkes_compensator_differences(fit_eq)
sapply(cd_eq, function(x) c(KS = ks.test(x, "pexp")$p.value,
                            Ljung_Box = Box.test(x, type = "Ljung")$p.value))

                  M3-4          M4+
KS        0.0002077805 1.533784e-02
Ljung_Box 0.0000000000 5.157212e-10


QQ plots of the compensator differences for each stream against the \(\text{Exp}(1)\) distribution are shown below.

qq <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(cd_eq), function(nm) {
    pp <- ppoints(200)
    data.frame(stream = nm, theoretical = qexp(pp), observed = quantile(cd_eq[[nm]], pp))
}))
ggplot(qq, aes(x = theoretical, y = observed)) +
    geom_point() + geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, col = "red") +
    facet_wrap(~stream, scales = "free") + theme_minimal() +
    xlab("Theoretical quantiles, Exp(1)") + ylab("Observed quantiles")








The QQ plots show that the distribution of the compensator differences is reasonably close to \(\text{Exp}(1)\) for both streams (apart from the longest gaps between small earthquakes), so the KS tests reject the model mainly because there are a lot of data. The Ljung-Box tests, however, give very small p-values: short gaps tend to follow short gaps, so the model is not fully capturing the clustering of earthquakes. As for the univariate and marked models (Section 3.4), the likely reasons are that exponential decay is too simple to describe aftershock sequences and that (as discussed above) the constraint on \(\alpha_{12}\) prevents a large earthquake from triggering many small ones.




Zaatour, Riadh. 2014. hawkes: Hawkes Process Simulation and Calibration Toolkit. https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=hawkes.

title: 5  Meshes
text:
5.1 What is the mesh for?
All of the spatial models in stelfi (the LGCPs of Chapter 6 and Chapter 7, and the spatiotemporal self-exciting models of Chapter 8) need a mesh: a triangulation of the study region. This chapter describes what the mesh is used for, how to build one, and how to check whether it is any good, both geometrically (using meshmetrics()) and for the data at hand.
A Gaussian random field \(G(s)\) is a continuous surface, so it cannot be estimated directly. The SPDE approach of Lindgren, Rue, and Lindström (2011) represents it by its values at the nodes (vertices) of a triangulation of the study region, and interpolates linearly between the nodes within each triangle. The field is then described by a finite number of values (one per node), and these have a multivariate normal distribution with a sparse precision matrix built from the geometry of the triangles. This is what makes fitting fast.
The mesh therefore controls
Note that the mesh is only used to represent the random field (and to approximate the integral of the intensity over the study region). The study region itself is given by the sf argument of the fit_*() functions, and the parts of the mesh outside it do not contribute any area.

title: 5  Meshes
5  Meshes
text:
5.2 Building a mesh
In stelfi (and inlabru) meshes are built using the fmesher package. The key arguments of fmesher::fm_mesh_2d() are:

loc: locations (usually the observed events) that the mesh is built around, so there are mesh nodes close to the data;
boundary: (optional) a polygon the mesh should follow, typically the study region (converted using fmesher::fm_as_segm()). Alternatively loc.domain gives a set of points whose convex hull is used, and offset how far beyond it the mesh should extend;
max.edge: the largest allowed triangle edge length. A vector of length two, c(inner, outer), gives a finer mesh inside the region and a coarser mesh in an outer extension, which reduces the inflated variance of the field near the edge of the mesh;
cutoff: the minimum allowed distance between nodes. Locations closer together than this share a node, which avoids lots of tiny triangles where events are clustered; and
min.angle: the smallest allowed interior angle of a triangle (21° by default, see Section 5.3).

The units of max.edge, cutoff and offset are those of the coordinates, so they should be chosen relative to the size of the study region (and, ideally, the range of the field). To illustrate, 100 locations are simulated uniformly in a 10 by 10 square and three meshes are built around them: one with only loc given, one with a finer inner and coarser outer part, and one where the cutoff is larger.

set.seed(1)
pts <- data.frame(x = runif(100, 0, 10), y = runif(100, 0, 10))
mesh_default <- fmesher::fm_mesh_2d(loc = as.matrix(pts))
mesh_inner_outer <- fmesher::fm_mesh_2d(loc = as.matrix(pts), max.edge = c(1, 3), offset = c(1, 3))
mesh_cutoff <- fmesher::fm_mesh_2d(loc = as.matrix(pts), max.edge = c(1, 3), offset = c(1, 3),
                                   cutoff = 1)
c(default = mesh_default$n, inner_outer = mesh_inner_outer$n, cutoff = mesh_cutoff$n) ## nodes

    default inner_outer      cutoff 
        205         493         158 


The meshes are converted to sf objects using mesh_2_sf() so that they can be plotted with ggplot2.

plot_mesh <- function(mesh, title) {
    ggplot() + geom_sf(data = mesh_2_sf(mesh), fill = NA, linewidth = 0.2) +
        geom_point(data = pts, aes(x = x, y = y), col = "red", size = 0.8) +
        theme_void() + ggtitle(title)
}
patchwork::wrap_plots(
    plot_mesh(mesh_default, "loc only"),
    plot_mesh(mesh_inner_outer, "max.edge = c(1, 3), offset = c(1, 3)"),
    plot_mesh(mesh_cutoff, "... and cutoff = 1"),
    nrow = 1)








With only loc the mesh simply joins up the locations (with some extra nodes added to avoid small angles), so the triangles are of very different sizes and the mesh stops at the convex hull of the data. Setting max.edge and offset gives triangles of a more even size and an outer extension with larger triangles. Increasing cutoff merges nearby locations, giving fewer nodes, at the cost of no longer having a node at every event.

5.2.1 How fine should the mesh be?
There is a trade-off. A mesh that is too coarse cannot capture spatial variation at a scale smaller than its triangles, while a mesh that is too fine is slow and memory-hungry and can make fitting unstable. A common rule of thumb is that max.edge (inner) should be no more than about a fifth of the range of the field, and that the outer extension should be at least about the range, so that the edge effects do not reach the study region. Since the range is not known before fitting, it is good practice to fit the model using a few meshes and check that the conclusions do not change. This is done for the terrorism events in Iraq (Section 6.3.2) in Sensitivity to the mesh, which also shows what can happen when the data have spatial structure at every scale.

title: 5  Meshes
section: 5.3 Checking the quality of a mesh
text:
5.3 Checking the quality of a mesh
Even if the mesh is fine enough for the data, poorly shaped triangles can cause numerical problems. The precision matrix of the field is built from matrices whose entries depend on the cotangents of the interior angles of the triangles, and these become very large as an angle approaches 0° (or 180°). Long thin triangles, or neighbouring triangles of very different sizes, can therefore make the precision matrix badly conditioned, the optimiser unstable, and the interpolated field a poor approximation of a smooth surface.
The function meshmetrics() takes a mesh and returns an sf object with one row per triangle (in the same order as mesh$graph$tv) and the following columns:

Here \(l_{\min}\) is the length of the shortest edge and \(L_1, L_2, L_3\) are the lengths of the three edges. Each of these is described below, using the example mesh horse_mesh (see Chapter 10).

data("horse_mesh", package = "stelfi")
data("horse_sf", package = "stelfi")
metrics <- meshmetrics(horse_mesh)
head(sf::st_drop_geometry(metrics)[, c("ID", "angleA", "angleB", "angleC", "radius_edge",
                                        "radius_ratio", "area", "quality")])

  ID   angleA   angleB   angleC radius_edge radius_ratio      area   quality
1  1 72.52737 56.41726 51.05537   0.6428770    0.4819599 1.2638698 0.9692923
2  2 55.86943 72.66586 51.46472   0.6392025    0.4820210 0.8832081 0.9695813
3  3 63.57095 65.27823 51.15083   0.6420134    0.4905740 0.9632860 0.9825119
4  4 65.92947 75.46785 38.60267   0.8013899    0.4402754 0.5677013 0.8843856
5  5 66.89736 56.55132 56.55132   0.5992474    0.4947592 0.4883824 0.9909965
6  6 61.46106 60.53316 58.00578   0.5895520    0.4995094 1.1719528 0.9991213



5.3.1 Interior angles
The interior angles are the most direct description of the shape of a triangle: an equilateral triangle has three angles of 60°, and a “sliver” (a long thin triangle) has at least one very small angle. Of all the possible triangulations of a set of points, the Delaunay triangulation is the one that maximises the smallest angle, but even so it can contain very small angles (see below). fmesher therefore refines the triangulation, adding extra nodes until no angle is smaller than min.angle (21° by default) and no edge is longer than max.edge, where possible. The smallest angle of each triangle is therefore a good first check:

min_angle <- pmin(metrics$angleA, metrics$angleB, metrics$angleC)
summary(min_angle)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  21.00   39.04   44.93   44.43   50.49   59.92 


As expected, no angle in horse_mesh is smaller than 21°.


5.3.2 The circumcircle and incircle
A triangle’s circumcircle is the unique circle that passes through all three of its vertices, and its incircle is the largest circle that fits inside it (i.e., that touches all three edges). Their radii are the circumradius \(R\) and the inradius \(r\), and their centres are the circumcentre and incentre. The circles of two triangles from horse_mesh are shown below: a well shaped triangle (left) and the worst shaped triangle in the mesh (right).

circle <- function(x, y, radius, n = 100) {
    a <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = n)
    data.frame(x = x + radius * cos(a), y = y + radius * sin(a))
}
plot_circles <- function(id) {
    tri <- metrics[metrics$ID == id, ]
    ggplot() +
        geom_path(data = circle(tri$c_Ox, tri$c_Oy, tri$circumcircle_R), aes(x = x, y = y),
                  col = "blue") +
        geom_path(data = circle(tri$i_Ox, tri$i_Oy, tri$incircle_r), aes(x = x, y = y),
                  col = "red") +
        geom_sf(data = tri, fill = NA, linewidth = 1) +
        geom_point(aes(x = tri$c_Ox, y = tri$c_Oy), col = "blue") +
        geom_point(aes(x = tri$i_Ox, y = tri$i_Oy), col = "red") +
        theme_void() + ggtitle(paste0("Triangle ", id, ", quality = ", round(tri$quality, 2)))
}
patchwork::wrap_plots(plot_circles(which.max(metrics$quality)),
                      plot_circles(which.min(metrics$quality)), nrow = 1)








The incentre (red) always lies inside the triangle, but the circumcentre (blue) lies outside it whenever the triangle has an obtuse angle (greater than 90°). The circumcircles are central to how meshes are built: in a Delaunay triangulation no node lies inside the circumcircle of any triangle, and the refinement algorithm improves a badly shaped triangle by adding a node at its circumcentre.
The radii are not very useful on their own, since they depend on the size of the triangle as well as its shape, but the two ratios below do not.


5.3.3 The radius-edge ratio
The radius-edge ratio, \(R/l_{\min}\), is the circumradius divided by the length of the shortest edge. It is smallest, \(1/\sqrt{3} \approx 0.577\), for an equilateral triangle and it is unbounded above: it becomes very large for a sliver, whose short edge is small compared with the circle through its vertices. In two dimensions it is directly related to the smallest angle \(\theta_{\min}\) of the triangle,
\[\frac{R}{l_{\min}} = \frac{1}{2 \sin \theta_{\min}},\]
so a bound on the smallest angle is the same as a bound on the radius-edge ratio. This is the measure used by mesh refinement algorithms: a minimum angle of 21° corresponds to a radius-edge ratio of at most \(1/(2\sin 21°) \approx\) 1.395.

summary(metrics$radius_edge)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
 0.5778  0.6481  0.7079  0.7440  0.7938  1.3952 

all.equal(metrics$radius_edge, 1 / (2 * sin(min_angle * pi / 180)))

[1] TRUE




5.3.4 The radius ratio
The radius ratio, \(r/R\), is the inradius divided by the circumradius. The incircle can never be more than half the size of the circumcircle, so the radius ratio is at most \(1/2\), for an equilateral triangle, and it tends to 0 as the triangle becomes degenerate. Unlike the radius-edge ratio it depends on all three angles, \(r/R = 4\sin\frac{A}{2}\sin\frac{B}{2}\sin\frac{C}{2}\), and it is bounded, so it is easier to compare between meshes and to plot on a common scale.

summary(metrics$radius_ratio)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
 0.2009  0.4137  0.4535  0.4404  0.4804  0.5000 




5.3.5 Area
The area of each triangle describes the resolution of the mesh rather than the shape of its triangles. Within the study region the triangles should be small compared with the range of the field (Section 5.2.1), and their size should change gradually: a large triangle next to a small one means the field is represented with very different precision in neighbouring places. Larger triangles in the outer extension of the mesh are intended, as the field there is only needed to reduce edge effects. Note that the area is in the squared units of the coordinates (e.g., km\(^2\)).


5.3.6 Quality
The quality measure,
\[\frac{4\sqrt{3}A}{\sum_{i = 1}^3 L_i^2},\]
compares the area of the triangle with the sum of its squared edge lengths. The constant \(4\sqrt{3}\) makes it equal to 1 for an equilateral triangle (the triangle with the largest area for a given sum of squared edges), and it tends to 0 for a degenerate triangle. Like the radius ratio it depends on all three angles and lies between 0 and 1, so it is a convenient single summary of the shape of each triangle.


5.3.7 Comparing the metrics
In two dimensions a triangle can only be badly shaped by having a small angle, so all of the shape measures above flag the same triangles; they differ in how they rank triangles that are not degenerate. The plot below shows the measures for every triangle in horse_mesh against the smallest angle.

m_df <- sf::st_drop_geometry(metrics)
m_df$min_angle <- min_angle
patchwork::wrap_plots(
    ggplot(m_df, aes(x = min_angle, y = radius_edge)) + geom_point(size = 0.8) +
        xlab("Smallest angle (degrees)") + ylab("Radius-edge ratio") + theme_minimal(),
    ggplot(m_df, aes(x = min_angle, y = radius_ratio)) + geom_point(size = 0.8) +
        xlab("Smallest angle (degrees)") + ylab("Radius ratio") + theme_minimal(),
    ggplot(m_df, aes(x = min_angle, y = quality)) + geom_point(size = 0.8) +
        xlab("Smallest angle (degrees)") + ylab("Quality") + theme_minimal(),
    nrow = 1)








The radius-edge ratio is a function of the smallest angle alone, whereas for the radius ratio and quality there is some spread for a given smallest angle, because they also depend on the other two angles.
Mapping the metrics is a quick way to see where the badly shaped or unusually sized triangles are. For horse_mesh the triangles are of a fairly even size and all are reasonably well shaped.

patchwork::wrap_plots(
    ggplot(metrics, aes(fill = area)) + geom_sf() + theme_void() +
        scale_fill_viridis_c() + ggtitle("Area"),
    ggplot(metrics, aes(fill = quality)) + geom_sf() + theme_void() +
        scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = c(0, 1)) + ggtitle("Quality"),
    nrow = 1)










5.3.8 A poorly shaped mesh
For comparison, below is the plain Delaunay triangulation of the 100 simulated locations from above (built using fmesher::fm_delaunay_2d(), which does not refine the triangulation), alongside a refined mesh around the same locations. The plain triangulation has many slivers, particularly around the edge of the data where the convex hull is joined up by long thin triangles.

mesh_delaunay <- fmesher::fm_delaunay_2d(as.matrix(pts))
mesh_refined <- fmesher::fm_mesh_2d(loc = as.matrix(pts), max.edge = 2, cutoff = 0.3)
metrics_delaunay <- meshmetrics(mesh_delaunay)
metrics_refined <- meshmetrics(mesh_refined)
patchwork::wrap_plots(
    ggplot(metrics_delaunay, aes(fill = quality)) + geom_sf() + theme_void() +
        scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = c(0, 1)) + ggtitle("Delaunay triangulation"),
    ggplot(metrics_refined, aes(fill = quality)) + geom_sf() + theme_void() +
        scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = c(0, 1)) + ggtitle("Refined mesh"),
    nrow = 1, guides = "collect")








The distributions of the metrics make the difference clear:

summarise_metrics <- function(m) {
    min_angle <- pmin(m$angleA, m$angleB, m$angleC)
    c(triangles = nrow(m), min_angle = min(min_angle), max_radius_edge = max(m$radius_edge),
      min_radius_ratio = min(m$radius_ratio), min_quality = min(m$quality),
      prop_quality_below_0.5 = mean(m$quality < 0.5))
}
round(rbind(delaunay = summarise_metrics(metrics_delaunay),
            refined = summarise_metrics(metrics_refined)), 3)

         triangles min_angle max_radius_edge min_radius_ratio min_quality
delaunay       189      0.36          79.678            0.000        0.01
refined        272     21.00           1.395            0.177        0.51
         prop_quality_below_0.5
delaunay                  0.344
refined                   0.000




5.3.9 What to look for
There is no single threshold that makes a mesh “good”, but the following are useful checks:

Shape. With the default refinement no angle is smaller than 21°, which gives a radius-edge ratio of at most about 1.4 and, in practice, a quality above about 0.5. Many triangles with quality well below this, particularly inside the study region, suggest that the mesh was built without refinement or with constraints (e.g., a very detailed boundary, or a small cutoff with clustered locations) that the refinement could not satisfy.
Size. Inside the study region the triangles should be small compared with the range of the field, and change in size gradually. Very small triangles (e.g., from a tiny cutoff where events are clustered) add nodes, and computation, without adding much information.
Location. Badly shaped triangles in the outer extension matter much less than those inside the study region, where the data are. The metrics can be restricted to the triangles that overlap the study region using sf, as below for horse_mesh and the polygon horse_sf it was built from.


inside <- lengths(sf::st_intersects(metrics, horse_sf)) > 0
summary(metrics$quality[inside])

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
 0.5441  0.8530  0.9182  0.8963  0.9638  1.0000 


If a mesh has poorly shaped triangles, increasing cutoff (so that clustered locations share nodes), simplifying a very detailed boundary (e.g., using sf::st_simplify()), or adjusting max.edge and offset usually helps. Once the mesh is well shaped, check that it is fine enough for the data by refitting the model on a few meshes (see Sensitivity to the mesh in Section 6.3.2).

title: 6  Spatial and spatiotemporal log-Gaussian Cox processes
text:
6.1 The model and your data
A log-Gaussian Cox process (LGCP) is a model for the locations of events in a study region. Unlike a Hawkes process, events do not cause other events. Instead, the intensity (the expected number of events per unit area) varies smoothly over space because of some unobserved environmental “surface”: events are more common where the surface is high and rarer where it is low. In the simplest case the intensity at location \(s\) is
\[\lambda(s) = \text{exp}(\beta_0 + G(s)), \tag{6.1}\]
where \(\beta_0\) is the intercept, the log intensity at an “average” location, and \(G(s)\) is a Gaussian random field, a smooth random surface with mean zero. Because \(G(s)\) is estimated from the data, the model can capture spatial clustering of events without you having to explain where it comes from. Covariates (e.g., population density) can be added to the log intensity, \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1(s) + ... + G(s)\), and the random field then captures the spatial variation that the covariates do not explain.
Plotted below is a realisation of an LGCP within a disc shaped region, overlain on the random field \(G(s)\): events are more common where the field is high (yellow).
Code for this figure
sf <- sf::st_as_sf(spatstat.geom::disc())
smesh <- fmesher::fm_mesh_2d(loc.domain = sf::st_coordinates(sf)[, 1:2], max.edge = 0.2, cutoff = 0.1)
set.seed(1)
sim <- sim_lgcp(parameters = c(beta = 3, log_tau = 1.6, log_kappa = 1.95), sf = sf, smesh = smesh)
pts <- smesh$loc[rep(1:nrow(smesh$loc), times = sim$y), 1:2]
set.seed(23)
pts <- data.frame(x = pts[, 1] + runif(nrow(pts), -0.05, 0.05), y = pts[, 2] + runif(nrow(pts), -0.05, 0.05))
pts <- pts[spatstat.geom::inside.owin(pts, w = spatstat.geom::disc()), ]
show_field(sim$x, smesh, sf = sf, clip = TRUE) + theme_void() + theme(legend.position = "none") +
    geom_point(data = pts, aes(x = x, y = y), size = 2)
The random field is described by two parameters, which stelfi reports on an interpretable scale:
Internally the field is parameterised by \(\tau\) and \(\kappa\), so get_coefs() reports log_tau and log_kappa (the parameters that are actually estimated) along with range \(= \sqrt{8}/\kappa\) and stdev \(= 1/\sqrt{4\pi\kappa^2\tau^2}\). Following Lindgren, Rue, and Lindström (2011), the field has a Matérn covariance function with smoothness \(\nu = 1\), and it is represented using the stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) approach on a triangulation (a mesh) of the study region.
The mesh controls how finely the field can vary in space and how much computation is needed, so it is an important part of fitting any spatial model in stelfi. How to build a mesh, and how to check whether it is adequate, is covered in Chapter 5.

title: 6  Spatial and spatiotemporal log-Gaussian Cox processes
text:
the range \(r\), the distance at which the correlation between values of the field drops to about 0.1. A small range means the intensity varies over short distances (small “hot spots”), a large range means it varies smoothly over large distances; and
the standard deviation \(\sigma\) of the field, how much the log intensity varies from place to place. For example \(\sigma = 1\) means that, on the log scale, the intensity typically varies by \(\pm 1\) from \(\beta_0\), i.e., by a factor of about \(e^{1} \approx 2.7\).




6.1.1 What your data need to look like
fit_lgcp() needs three things:

locs, a data frame of event locations with columns named x and y (and t for a spatiotemporal model, Section 6.5);
sf, an sf polygon of the study region; and
smesh, a mesh (Chapter 5).

Things to be aware of:

Use a projected coordinate system. The field is defined in terms of distances, so longitude and latitude (in degrees) should be projected to a planar coordinate system (e.g., UTM) using sf::st_transform(). Working in kilometres rather than metres keeps the numbers well scaled and makes the parameters easy to interpret: the intensity is then per km\(^2\) and the range is in km. The events, the study region and the mesh must all be in the same coordinates (it is often easiest to drop the CRS once everything is projected, see Section 6.3.2).
The study region should be where events could have been observed. The model assumes that every part of the study region was observed with equal effort. If, for example, sightings can only be made where there are people, then the intensity estimates the rate of reported events, and the random field will pick up variation in observation effort as well as variation in the underlying process. Including a covariate that describes effort (e.g., population density) can help. Events outside the study region are ignored.
Events are summarised by mesh node. stelfi counts the number of events closest to each mesh node (i.e., in each cell of the “dual” mesh) and models these counts. Detail at scales smaller than the mesh triangles is therefore lost, which is another reason to check that results are not sensitive to the mesh.
Duplicate locations are allowed for fitting (unlike tied times in a Hawkes process), but they need to be jittered for some of the goodness-of-fit checks (Section 6.4).
Covariates must be given at the mesh nodes, as a matrix with one row per mesh node (smesh$n rows) and one column per covariate. If your covariate is a raster or is only known at some locations, it needs to be extracted or interpolated at the mesh nodes, see Section 6.3.2.
Events do not interact. An LGCP describes clustering caused by a smooth environment, not clustering caused by events triggering each other. If the latter is plausible, consider a spatiotemporal self-exciting model (Chapter 8).
Number of events. The field parameters (in particular the range) are hard to estimate with few events or when the range is large relative to the study region. A few hundred events is a reasonable minimum.

6.2 A simulated example
Data were simulated from an LGCP (using spatstat, Baddeley, Rubak, and Turner (2015)) within a disc of radius 1, with intercept \(\beta_0 = 4\), field standard deviation \(\sigma = 1\), and range \(r = \sqrt{8} \times 0.2 \approx\) 0.566. In spatstat.random::rLGCP() the field has a Matérn covariance with smoothness nu \(= 1\) (the same as in stelfi), mu is the intercept, var is the variance of the field (\(\sigma^2\)), and scale is \(1/\kappa\), so that the range is \(\sqrt{8} \times\) scale.

win <- spatstat.geom::disc()
set.seed(1234)
sim <- spatstat.random::rLGCP("matern", mu = 4, var = 1, scale = 0.2, nu = 1, win = win)
locs <- data.frame(x = sim$x, y = sim$y)
truth <- c(beta = 4, range = sqrt(8) * 0.2, sigma = 1)

The data are a data frame of 272 event locations:

3  0.2112133  0.8551978

5  0.2303162 -0.8321345
6 -0.4731538  0.5615277


The study region is a disc of radius 1, which is converted to an sf polygon. The plot below shows the events and the true (simulated) random field.

sf <- sf::st_sf(geometry = sf::st_geometry(sf::st_as_sf(spatstat.geom::disc())))



Code for this figure
xs <- attr(sim, "Lambda")$xcol; ys <- attr(sim, "Lambda")$yrow
pxl <- expand.grid(x = xs, y = ys)
pxl$rf <- log(as.vector(t(attr(sim, "Lambda")$v))) - 4 ## minus the intercept
ggplot() +
    geom_tile(data = pxl, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = rf)) +
    labs(fill = "G(s)") + xlab("") + ylab("") +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "D", na.value = NA) +
    coord_equal() + theme_void() +
    geom_sf(data = sf, fill = NA, linewidth = 1) +
    geom_point(data = locs, aes(x = x, y = y), size = 0.8)










6.2.1 Fitting the model using stelfi
First a mesh is built around the events (Chapter 5). Here max.edge is 0.1 inside the region, about a fifth of the true range.

smesh <- fmesher::fm_mesh_2d(loc = locs[, 1:2], max.edge = c(0.1, 0.3), cutoff = 0.03)
smesh$n ## number of mesh nodes

[1] 1124


The model is fitted using fit_lgcp() with starting values for \(\beta_0\) (beta), \(\log(\tau)\) (log_tau) and \(\log(\kappa)\) (log_kappa). A sensible starting value for the intercept is the log of the average number of events per unit area.

area <- as.numeric(sf::st_area(sf))
fit <- fit_lgcp(locs = locs, sf = sf, smesh = smesh,
                parameters = c(beta = log(nrow(locs) / area), log_tau = log(1), log_kappa = log(1)))
stelfi <- get_coefs(fit)
stelfi

            Estimate Std. Error
beta       4.1456922  0.1798657
log_tau   -3.2271510  0.2588465
log_kappa  2.2036142  0.2577273
range      0.3122680  0.0804800
stdev      0.7850755  0.1059713


The estimated random field is extracted using get_fields() and plotted using show_field(). Compare this with the true field above.

get_fields(fit, smesh) |>
    show_field(smesh = smesh, sf = sf, clip = TRUE) + theme_void() +
    geom_point(data = locs, aes(x = x, y = y), size = 0.8)










6.2.2 Comparison with inlabru and spatstat
The same model is fitted below using inlabru (Bachl et al. (2019)) and spatstat (Baddeley, Rubak, and Turner (2015)). When comparing the results bear in mind that:

stelfi uses maximum likelihood (the field is integrated out using the Laplace approximation) so there are no priors and the estimates have standard errors.
inlabru is Bayesian (using INLA), so priors are needed for the field and it reports posterior means and standard deviations. Penalised complexity priors are used via inla.spde2.pcmatern(): prior.range = c(0.05, 0.01) means \(P(r < 0.05) = 0.01\) and prior.sigma = c(5, 0.01) means \(P(\sigma > 5) = 0.01\), both deliberately weak. To make inlabru as close as possible to a maximum likelihood fit, the hyperparameters are not integrated over (int.strategy = "eb"). The same mesh is used for both.
spatstat fits the model by minimum contrast, matching the theoretical \(K\) function of the LGCP to the empirical one. This does not use a mesh and does not give standard errors. Its Matérn scale parameter (reported as alpha in modelpar) is \(1/\kappa\), so the range is \(\sqrt{8} \times\) scale, and it reports the variance sigma2 rather than the standard deviation.

Note that inlabru requires the geometry column of the study region to be called geometry, which is why sf was created using sf::st_sf(geometry = ...) above.

library(inlabru)
library(INLA)
sf_locs <- sf::st_as_sf(locs, coords = c("x", "y"))
matern <- INLA::inla.spde2.pcmatern(smesh, prior.range = c(0.05, 0.01), prior.sigma = c(5, 0.01))
cmp <- geometry ~ field(geometry, model = matern) + Intercept(1)
fit_bru <- lgcp(cmp, sf_locs, samplers = sf, domain = list(geometry = smesh),
                options = bru_options(control.inla = list(int.strategy = "eb")))
bru <- rbind(fit_bru$summary.fixed[, 1:2], fit_bru$summary.hyperpar[, 1:2])

6.3 Applied examples

6.3.1 Sasquatch sightings in the USA
The sasquatch data (see Chapter 10) are the locations of 972 reported sasquatch (bigfoot) sightings in the contiguous USA between 2000 and 2005, collated by the Bigfoot Field Researchers Organization. This example is also used in Jones-Todd and van Helsdingen (2024).

Preparing the data
The sightings are given as longitude/latitude. They, and the boundary of the contiguous USA (from the maps package), are projected to the Conus Albers projection (EPSG:5070) and converted from metres to kilometres.

data("sasquatch", package = "stelfi")
sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)
## boundary of the contiguous USA: projected and in km
us <- maps::map("usa", fill = TRUE, plot = FALSE) |>
    sf::st_as_sf() |>
    sf::st_make_valid() |>
    sf::st_transform(crs = 5070)
us_km <- sf::st_sf(geometry = sf::st_union(sf::st_geometry(us)) / 1000)
## sighting locations: projected and in km
locs_sq <- sf::st_transform(sasquatch, crs = 5070) |>
    sf::st_coordinates() |>
    as.data.frame()
names(locs_sq) <- c("x", "y")
locs_sq <- locs_sq / 1000
head(locs_sq)

          x        y

3 -398.2722 2817.326
4 -505.9007 2766.177

Fitting the model
The mesh has a maximum edge length of 200 km (the contiguous USA is about 4500 km across).

smesh_km <- fmesher::fm_mesh_2d(loc = locs_sq[, 1:2], max.edge = c(200, 500), cutoff = 100)
area_sq <- as.numeric(sf::st_area(us_km))
fit_sq <- fit_lgcp(locs = locs_sq, sf = us_km, smesh = smesh_km,
                   parameters = c(beta = log(nrow(locs_sq) / area_sq),
                                  log_tau = log(1), log_kappa = log(1)))
coefs <- get_coefs(fit_sq)
coefs

            Estimate  Std. Error
beta       -9.937128   0.3865470
log_tau     4.046748   0.1069927
log_kappa  -5.662232   0.1818064
range     813.993537 147.9892483
stdev       1.419028   0.1880643


From these estimates, the range of the field is around 814 km, so sightings are clustered at a regional scale, and the standard deviation of 1.42 means the intensity of sightings varies by a large factor between regions. The estimated random field and the estimated intensity (expected number of sightings per km\(^2\)) are plotted using show_field() and show_lambda().

get_fields(fit_sq, smesh_km) |>
    show_field(smesh = smesh_km, sf = us_km, clip = TRUE) + theme_void()









show_lambda(fit_sq, smesh = smesh_km, sf = us_km, clip = TRUE) + theme_void()








The hot spots (e.g., the Pacific Northwest) are clear. Remember, though, that these are reported sightings: the model cannot distinguish places where sasquatch are common from places where many people are out looking for them (Section 6.1.1).



6.3.2 Terrorism events in Iraq
The iraq_terrorism data (see Chapter 10) are the locations and dates of terrorism events in Iraq carried out by ISIL between 2013 and 2017. This example shows the full stelfi workflow for a region with an awkward boundary, compares stelfi with inlabru on several meshes, explores how sensitive the results are to the mesh, and includes covariates in the intensity. A spatiotemporal version is in Section 6.5.3.

Preparing the data
The event locations are projected to UTM zone 38N (EPSG:32638), which covers most of Iraq, and converted to kilometres. The boundary of Iraq is obtained from the rnaturalearth package and transformed in the same way.

data("iraq_terrorism", package = "stelfi")
## event locations (lon/lat) -> UTM zone 38N -> km
locs_km <- as.data.frame(sf::st_coordinates(sf::st_transform(iraq_terrorism, crs = 32638)) / 1000)
names(locs_km) <- c("x", "y")
## the boundary of Iraq in the same coordinates
iraq_sf <- rnaturalearth::ne_countries(country = "Iraq", scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf") |>
    sf::st_transform(crs = 32638) |>
    sf::st_union()                     ## collapse to a single polygon
iraq_sf_km <- sf::st_sf(geometry = sf::st_geometry(iraq_sf) / 1000)
## once in km the coordinates are just planar numbers, so drop the CRS
## so that the events, the boundary and the mesh are all treated consistently
sf::st_crs(iraq_sf_km) <- NA
points_km <- sf::st_as_sf(locs_km, coords = c("x", "y")) ## used by inlabru



Building the meshes
To show how much the mesh matters, three very different meshes are built. Each follows the boundary of Iraq (boundary), is placed around the events, and has a finer inner and coarser outer part (max.edge = c(inner, outer)).

Too coarse (max.edge = c(200, 400), cutoff = 100): triangles a couple of hundred km across, larger than many of the clusters of attacks;
Adequate (max.edge = c(40, 150), cutoff = 20): triangles a few tens of km across. The relatively large cutoff means that events in the same town share a node, so there are no very small triangles; and
Too fine (max.edge = c(10, 100), cutoff = 1): there is a node at almost every distinct event location, so there are many tiny triangles where attacks are clustered.


mesh_args <- list(too_coarse = list(max.edge = c(200, 400), cutoff = 100),
                  adequate   = list(max.edge = c(40, 150), cutoff = 20),
                  too_fine   = list(max.edge = c(10, 100), cutoff = 1))
meshes <- lapply(mesh_args, function(a) {
    fmesher::fm_mesh_2d(loc = locs_km[, 1:2],
                        boundary = fmesher::fm_as_segm(iraq_sf_km),
                        max.edge = a$max.edge, cutoff = a$cutoff)
})
## number of nodes, and the size of the triangles (km^2)
t(sapply(meshes, function(m) {
    area <- as.numeric(sf::st_area(mesh_2_sf(m)))
    c(nodes = m$n, triangles = length(area), median_area = round(median(area)),
      smallest_area = round(min(area), 2), below_10km2 = sum(area < 10))
}))

Fitting with stelfi
The model is fitted using each mesh, and the time taken (in seconds) is recorded using system.time().

area_km2 <- as.numeric(sf::st_area(iraq_sf_km))
beta_start <- log(nrow(locs_km) / area_km2)
start <- c(beta = beta_start, log_tau = log(1), log_kappa = log(1))

for (m in names(meshes)) {
    time_stelfi[m] <- system.time(
        fits_stelfi[[m]] <- fit_lgcp(locs = locs_km, sf = iraq_sf_km, smesh = meshes[[m]],
                                     parameters = start)
    )["elapsed"]
}
get_coefs(fits_stelfi$adequate)

The estimated random field and intensity surface (events per km\(^2\)) for the adequate mesh:

    show_field(smesh = meshes$adequate, sf = iraq_sf_km, clip = TRUE) + theme_void()

    theme_void()










Comparing with inlabru
The same model is fitted using inlabru on the same three meshes, with weak penalised complexity priors (\(P(r < 5\text{ km}) = 0.01\) and \(P(\sigma > 10) = 0.01\)) and empirical Bayes (see Section 6.2), again recording the time taken.

fit_bru <- function(mesh) {
    matern <- INLA::inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh, prior.sigma = c(10, 0.01), prior.range = c(5, 0.01))
    cmp <- geometry ~ mySmooth(geometry, model = matern) + Intercept(1)
    inlabru::lgcp(cmp, data = points_km, samplers = iraq_sf_km,
                  domain = list(geometry = mesh),
                  options = inlabru::bru_options(
                      control.inla = list(int.strategy = "eb", strategy = "gaussian",
                                          diagonal = 1e-4, control.vb = list(enable = FALSE))))
}
fits_inlabru <- list(); time_inlabru <- c()
for (m in names(meshes)) {
    time_inlabru[m] <- system.time(fits_inlabru[[m]] <- fit_bru(meshes[[m]]))["elapsed"]
}

patchwork::wrap_plots(lambdas, nrow = 1)









Too coarse. With only a few dozen nodes both fits are almost instant, but the triangles are larger than the clusters of attacks. The field can only vary smoothly over hundreds of km, so the estimated range is several hundred km, the hot spots are smeared out, and the intensity surface is blocky.
Too fine. With over ten thousand nodes both fits take far longer (here stelfi was the slower of the two for this mesh: TMB runs on a single thread by default, whereas INLA uses several). The field now resolves individual towns: the estimated range drops to a few km and the standard deviation increases, and the two packages disagree much more, since their approximations of the integral of the intensity over Iraq (stelfi assigns each event and each piece of area to its nearest mesh node, inlabru uses integration points) differ most when the mesh is this fine. Very little is gained for the extra computation: the large scale pattern of the intensity is the same as for the adequate mesh.
Adequate. The fits take a second or two, the intensity surface shows the hot spots around Baghdad and along the Tigris and Euphrates, and the two packages tell a similar story: a field with a large standard deviation (around 3, so the intensity varies by orders of magnitude across Iraq) and a range of around 100 km (inlabru’s is somewhat larger). The intercepts differ more between the packages, partly because of the different integration schemes and partly because the intercept is only weakly identified when the field is this variable.

Note that the estimated range does not settle down as the mesh is refined, for either package. The reason is the data: attacks are concentrated in particular towns and cities, so there is spatial structure at every scale down to a few kilometres, and whatever mesh is used the field picks up variation down to the smallest scale the mesh can represent. This also means that the rule of thumb of Section 5.2.1 (inner max.edge no more than about a fifth of the range) cannot be satisfied. In this situation:

the range should be interpreted as “the scale of variation resolved at this mesh”, and the mesh reported alongside the results;
choose the mesh to match the scale of the question being asked (e.g., differences between regions versus between neighbourhoods), avoiding many small triangles that add computation without changing the large scale pattern; and
consider whether the fine scale clustering is better explained by covariates (e.g., the locations of towns, population density) or by events triggering further events (Chapter 8).



Including covariates
Covariates are included in the log intensity, \(\lambda(s) = \text{exp}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1(s) + ... + G(s))\), using the covariates argument of fit_lgcp(). The covariates must be a matrix with one column per covariate and one row per mesh node, and the starting value beta becomes a vector: the intercept followed by one coefficient per covariate. It is a good idea to standardise covariates (using scale()), so that the coefficients are the change in log intensity per standard deviation increase in the covariate and the optimiser works with parameters on a similar scale. The adequate mesh is used below.

smesh <- meshes$adequate

Distance to Baghdad. Here the covariate is the distance (in km) from each mesh node to Baghdad (33.30°N, 44.40°E).

baghdad_dist <- sqrt((mesh_coords[, 1] - baghdad_km[1])^2 + (mesh_coords[, 2] - baghdad_km[2])^2)
