title: 6  Spatial and spatiotemporal log-Gaussian Cox processes
text:
6.4 Goodness-of-fit
A natural question is whether point patterns simulated from the fitted model look like the observed pattern. This can be checked by comparing summary functions of the observed pattern with those of patterns simulated from the fitted model, using spatstat (Baddeley, Rubak, and Turner (2015)). Two nearest-neighbour summaries are used here:

the \(G\) function, the distribution function of the distance from a typical event to its nearest other event. For a clustered pattern \(G(r)\) rises faster than for a completely random (Poisson) pattern since events tend to have a close neighbour; and
the \(F\) function (empty space function), the distribution function of the distance from an arbitrary location to the nearest event. For a clustered pattern \(F(r)\) rises more slowly than for a Poisson pattern since there are large empty gaps between clusters.

If the fitted LGCP is adequate, the observed curves should lie within the envelope formed by the curves of the simulated patterns. Distances must be measured in planar coordinates, so this is done for the sasquatch model (Section 6.3.1), which was fitted in km.

6.4.1 Preparing the observed pattern
The observed events are converted to a spatstat point pattern (ppp) within the study region (owin). Some sightings share exactly the same location, which gives nearest-neighbour distances of zero, so the pattern is jittered slightly using rjitter().

library(spatstat.geom)
library(spatstat.explore)
us_window <- as.owin(us_km)
set.seed(1)
obs_ppp <- ppp(x = locs_sq$x, y = locs_sq$y, window = us_window)
obs_ppp <- rjitter(obs_ppp, retry = TRUE)



6.4.2 Simulating from the fitted model
The function below simulates one point pattern from the fitted LGCP using sim_lgcp() and the estimated parameters. This simulates a new random field each time (the model is checked as a whole, not just the estimated field). sim_lgcp() returns the number of events per mesh node, so each node is repeated as many times as it has events and the resulting pattern is jittered (by half the mesh cutoff) so that events are spread around the node.

generate_simulated_ppp <- function() {
    sim <- sim_lgcp(sf = us_km, smesh = smesh_km,
                    parameters = c(beta = unname(coefs["beta", 1]),
                                   log_tau = unname(coefs["log_tau", 1]),
                                   log_kappa = unname(coefs["log_kappa", 1])))
    if (sum(sim$y) < 2) return(NULL) ## need two events for nearest-neighbour distances
    idx <- rep(1:nrow(smesh_km$loc), times = sim$y)
    sim_ppp <- ppp(x = smesh_km$loc[idx, 1], y = smesh_km$loc[idx, 2],
                   window = us_window, check = FALSE)
    rjitter(sim_ppp, radius = 50, retry = TRUE)
}



6.4.3 Simulation envelopes
A simulation envelope gives, for each distance \(r\), the range (here the minimum and maximum) of the summary function over many simulated patterns. With 39 simulations a pointwise envelope based on the minimum and maximum corresponds to a test with significance level \(2/(39 + 1) = 0.05\) at each \(r\) (more simulations, e.g., 99, are preferable but take longer). Passing the list of LGCP simulations to the simulate argument of envelope() is important, otherwise the envelope is formed from completely random patterns and instead tests whether there is any spatial structure at all.

set.seed(3)
sim_list <- lapply(1:39, function(i) generate_simulated_ppp())
sim_list <- Filter(Negate(is.null), sim_list)
g_envelope <- envelope(Y = obs_ppp, fun = Gest, simulate = sim_list,
                       nsim = length(sim_list), savefuns = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
plot(g_envelope, main = "Sasquatch LGCP: G function", xlab = "Distance (km)", legend = FALSE)









f_envelope <- envelope(Y = obs_ppp, fun = Fest, simulate = sim_list,
                       nsim = length(sim_list), savefuns = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
plot(f_envelope, main = "Sasquatch LGCP: F function", xlab = "Distance (km)", legend = FALSE)








In each plot the solid black line is the observed function, the dashed red line is the mean of the simulated patterns, and the grey band is the envelope. Where the observed curve leaves the band the fitted model is not reproducing that aspect of the data. Points to bear in mind when reading these plots:

at distances smaller than the mesh resolution (here about 100 to 200 km) the simulated patterns are only as realistic as the jittering used to spread events around their mesh node, so differences at very short distances say more about the mesh than about the model; and
the \(G\) function is about how close events are to each other. If events are much closer together than the model expects (more short nearest-neighbour distances), this suggests clustering at a finer scale than the field can capture, e.g., because events trigger one another (Chapter 8) or because of duplicated reports.

text:
6.5 Spatiotemporal LGCP

6.5.1 The model and your data
If the event locations are recorded over a period of time, the spatial pattern may change over time. A spatiotemporal LGCP allows this by having a separate random field at each of a set of time knots \(t_1, t_2, ..., t_K\):
\[\lambda_k(s) = \text{exp}(\beta_0 + G_k(s)),\]
where the fields are linked over time by a first order autoregressive (AR(1)) process,
\[G_k(s) = \rho\, G_{k-1}(s) + \epsilon_k(s),\]
and the \(\epsilon_k(s)\) are independent random fields. All of the fields share the same range and standard deviation. The new parameter is \(\rho\) (\(-1 < \rho < 1\)), the correlation between the fields at consecutive time knots: \(\rho\) close to 1 means the spatial pattern of events is very persistent over time, \(\rho\) close to 0 means the pattern at one knot is almost unrelated to the pattern at the previous one. get_coefs() reports rho along with the parameters of the spatial model, and atanh_rho is the transformed parameter used when giving starting values.
To fit the model you need, in addition to a spatial model (Section 6.1.1):

a column t in locs giving the time of each event; and
a temporal mesh tmesh, built using fmesher::fm_mesh_1d() with the knots as its argument, e.g., fmesher::fm_mesh_1d(0:5) for knots at \(t = 0, 1, ..., 5\).

Each event is assigned to its nearest time knot, so knot \(t_k\) covers the time period from halfway between \(t_{k-1}\) and \(t_k\) to halfway between \(t_k\) and \(t_{k+1}\), and the first and last knots cover only half a period. Things to be aware of:

The times and knots must be on the same scale. For example, if t is in years since the start of the study, the knots should be too. Check tmesh$loc to see the knots that were created.
All times must lie between the first and last knots (fit_lgcp() gives an error otherwise). For example, with yearly data starting at \(t = 0\) and finishing within year 5, use continuous (decimal) times and knots 0:5, so the last knot covers the final half year. Knots whose period contains no events are allowed, but they carry little information.
The cost grows with the number of knots, since there is a field at every knot: roughly the number of mesh nodes times the number of knots. A coarser spatial mesh than for a purely spatial model is often needed.



6.5.2 A simulated example
Data were simulated from a spatiotemporal LGCP within a disc of radius 2 over the time period \([0, 5)\), with \(\beta_0 = 2\), range \(r = 1\), standard deviation \(\sigma = 1\), and \(\rho = 0.7\), with one field per unit of time. The simulation has three steps:

Independent fields. At each of the \(K = 6\) time knots (\(t = 0, 1, ..., 5\)) an independent random field \(\epsilon_k(s)\) is simulated at the mesh nodes using sim_lgcp() (only the simulated field, $x, is used). sim_lgcp() takes the field parameters on the internal scale, so the range and standard deviation are first converted to \(\kappa = \sqrt{8}/r\) and \(\tau = 1/(\sigma\sqrt{4\pi}\kappa)\).
AR(1) fields. The fields are linked over time, \(G_k(s) = \rho\, G_{k-1}(s) + \sqrt{1 - \rho^2}\, \epsilon_k(s)\). The factor \(\sqrt{1 - \rho^2}\) keeps the standard deviation of every \(G_k(s)\) equal to \(\sigma\).
Events. The events in the time period covered by each knot (Section 6.5) are simulated by thinning: candidate events are simulated uniformly over the disc at the maximum of the intensity \(\lambda_{\max}\), and each candidate at location \(s\) is kept with probability \(\lambda_k(s)/\lambda_{\max}\), with the field at \(s\) interpolated from the mesh nodes using fmesher::fm_basis(). The kept events are given times drawn uniformly within the period.


disc_sf <- sf::st_sf(geometry = sf::st_geometry(sf::st_as_sf(spatstat.geom::disc(radius = 2))))
smesh <- fmesher::fm_mesh_2d(boundary = fmesher::fm_as_segm(disc_sf), max.edge = 0.2, cutoff = 0.05)
tmesh <- fmesher::fm_mesh_1d(0:5)
k <- tmesh$n
truth_st <- c(beta = 2, range = 1, sigma = 1, rho = 0.7)
kap <- unname(sqrt(8) / truth_st["range"]); tau <- unname(1 / (truth_st["sigma"] * sqrt(4 * pi) * kap))
set.seed(3)
## 1. independent fields, one column per time knot
e <- sapply(1:k, function(i)
    as.vector(sim_lgcp(c(beta = 0, log_tau = log(tau), log_kappa = log(kap)), sf = disc_sf, smesh = smesh)$x))
## 2. AR(1) fields
x <- e
for (i in 2:k) x[, i] <- truth_st["rho"] * x[, i - 1] + sqrt(1 - truth_st["rho"]^2) * e[, i]
## 3. events, by thinning, for the time period covered by each knot
locs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:k, function(i) {
    lo <- max(0, tmesh$loc[i] - 0.5); hi <- min(5, tmesh$loc[i] + 0.5)
    lmax <- exp(truth_st["beta"] + max(x[, i]))
    n0 <- rpois(1, lmax * 16 * (hi - lo)) ## candidates over the 4 by 4 square around the disc
    cand <- data.frame(x = runif(n0, -2, 2), y = runif(n0, -2, 2))
    cand <- cand[sqrt(cand$x^2 + cand$y^2) < 2, ]
    A <- fmesher::fm_basis(smesh, loc = as.matrix(cand))
    keep <- runif(nrow(cand)) < exp(truth_st["beta"] + as.vector(A %*% x[, i])) / lmax
    data.frame(cand[keep, ], t = runif(sum(keep), lo, hi))
}))
locs <- locs[locs$t < 5, ]
locs <- locs[order(locs$t), ]
rownames(locs) <- NULL

6.5.3 An applied example: terrorism events in Iraq by year
The iraq_terrorism data (Section 6.3.2) also record the year, month and day of each event, so the intensity can be allowed to change over time. Here time is measured in years since the start of 2013 (as a decimal, using the month and day) and there is one knot per year.

locs_st <- as.data.frame(sf::st_coordinates(sf::st_transform(iraq_terrorism, crs = 32638)) / 1000)
names(locs_st) <- c("x", "y")
locs_st$t <- (iraq_terrorism$iyear - 2013) + (iraq_terrorism$imonth - 1) / 12 +
    (iraq_terrorism$iday - 1) / 365
locs_st <- locs_st[order(locs_st$t), ]
range(locs_st$t)

[1] 0.2965753 4.9988584


The spatial mesh follows the boundary of Iraq and is coarser than for the spatial model because there are six fields to estimate. The temporal knots are at \(t = 0, 1, ..., 5\) (the start of each year), so the final knot covers the second half of 2017.

smesh_st <- fmesher::fm_mesh_2d(boundary = fmesher::fm_as_segm(iraq_sf_km), max.edge = 50, cutoff = 20)
smesh_st$n

[1] 496

tmesh_st <- fmesher::fm_mesh_1d(0:5)

Starting values matter for this model. For the intercept, the log of the average number of events per km\(^2\) per year is a sensible start. For the range a starting value of around 300 km is used (\(\kappa = \sqrt{8}/300\)).

n_years <- 5
start <- c(beta = log(nrow(locs_st) / (area_km2 * n_years)),
           log_tau = log(0.1), log_kappa = log(sqrt(8) / 300), atanh_rho = 0.2)
fit_iraq_st <- fit_lgcp(locs = locs_st, sf = iraq_sf_km, smesh = smesh_st, tmesh = tmesh_st,
                        parameters = start)
coefs_st <- get_coefs(fit_iraq_st)

plots <- lapply(1:6, function(k) {

If the model does not converge, things to try are a coarser spatial mesh, fewer knots, different starting values (in particular beta, log_tau and atanh_rho), or fitting a spatial LGCP (Section 6.3.2) to each year first to get an idea of sensible values for \(\beta_0\), \(\tau\), and \(\kappa\).


6.5.4 Goodness-of-fit
The simulation envelopes of Section 6.4 can be used for a single time period. Below a slightly different check is used: rather than simulating new random fields, events are simulated from the estimated intensity for one knot (an inhomogeneous Poisson process), and the \(G\) function of these is compared with that of the observed events in the corresponding period. This asks whether, given the estimated intensity surface, the events are more clustered than expected. Here the knot at \(t = 2\) (mid 2014 to mid 2015) is checked.

knot <- 3 ## the index of the knot at t = 2
in_period <- abs(locs_st$t - tmesh_st$loc[knot]) < 0.5
obs <- locs_st[in_period, ]
iraq_window <- as.owin(iraq_sf_km)
set.seed(1)
obs_ppp_st <- rjitter(ppp(obs$x, obs$y, window = iraq_window), retry = TRUE)
## estimated log intensity at the mesh nodes for this knot
eta <- coefs_st["beta", 1] + get_fields(fit_iraq_st, smesh_st, tmesh_st)[, knot]
## simulate from the estimated intensity (per km^2 per year) by thinning
sim_from_fitted <- function() {
    bb <- sf::st_bbox(iraq_sf_km)
    lmax <- exp(max(eta))
    n0 <- rpois(1, lmax * (bb["xmax"] - bb["xmin"]) * (bb["ymax"] - bb["ymin"]))
    cand <- ppp(runif(n0, bb["xmin"], bb["xmax"]), runif(n0, bb["ymin"], bb["ymax"]),
                window = owin(bb[c("xmin", "xmax")], bb[c("ymin", "ymax")]))
    cand <- cand[iraq_window]
    lambda <- exp(as.vector(fmesher::fm_basis(smesh_st, loc = cbind(cand$x, cand$y)) %*% eta))
    cand[runif(cand$n) < lambda / lmax]
}
sims <- lapply(1:39, function(i) sim_from_fitted())
g_env_st <- envelope(obs_ppp_st, fun = Gest, simulate = sims, nsim = 39, verbose = FALSE)


plot(g_env_st, main = "Iraq, t = 2: G function", xlab = "Distance (km)", legend = FALSE)








The observed \(G\) function lies well above the envelope at short distances: many events are much closer to another event than would be expected given the estimated intensity. This is not surprising: the mesh (and the knots) can only describe variation in intensity at scales of tens of kilometres and a year, whereas attacks are often concentrated in particular towns and occur in bursts. A finer mesh would help, but this kind of small scale clustering in space and time is also exactly what a self-exciting model is designed to capture, see Chapter 8.

title: 7  Marked log-Gaussian Cox process
text:
7.1 The model and your data
Often something is measured on each event as well as its location: the number of people killed in an attack, the size of a tree, or whether a disease case was severe. These measurements are called marks. A marked LGCP models the locations of the events and their marks together. This allows you to ask not only where events happen (as in Chapter 6) but also how the marks vary over space, and whether the marks are related to how many events there are (e.g., are attacks more deadly where attacks are more frequent?).
In stelfi the locations follow an LGCP exactly as in Chapter 6,
\[\lambda(s) = \text{exp}(\beta_{pp} + G_{pp}(s)),\]
where the subscript \(pp\) stands for “point process”. Each mark \(j\) then has its own linear predictor,
\[\eta_j(s) = \beta_{m_j} + \alpha_j \log \lambda(s) + G_{m_j}(s),\]
where \(\beta_{m_j}\) is the intercept for the mark, \(G_{m_j}(s)\) is an (optional) random field for the mark, \(\log \lambda(s) = \beta_{pp} + G_{pp}(s)\) is the log intensity of the point process, and \(\alpha_j\) links the mark to the point process: if \(\alpha_j > 0\) the mark tends to be larger where events are more common, if \(\alpha_j < 0\) it tends to be smaller, and if \(\alpha_j = 0\) the mark is unrelated to the intensity. The linear predictor is related to the mark through a distribution chosen using the methods argument:
get_coefs() reports the intercepts (betapp, betamarks), the link coefficients (marks_coefs_pp, the \(\alpha_j\)) and the parameters tau and kappa of each random field (the first for the point process). The range and standard deviation of each field are \(\sqrt{8}/\kappa\) and \(1/\sqrt{4\pi\kappa^2\tau^2}\), as in Chapter 6.

7.1.1 What your data need to look like
fit_mlgcp() needs everything that fit_lgcp() needs (Section 6.1.1) and some extra arguments:

locs, the event locations, a data frame (or matrix) with columns named x and y;
marks, a matrix with one row per event (in the same order as locs) and one column per mark, even if there is only one mark;
methods, a vector giving the distribution of each mark (see the table above);
fields, a vector of 0s and 1s, one per mark, saying whether each mark has its own random field \(G_{m_j}(s)\) (1, the default) or not (0). Without its own field, a mark depends on location only through \(\alpha_j \log \lambda(s)\);
strfixed, a matrix the same size as marks with the fixed structural parameter for each mark of each event (see the table above); and
parameters, a list of starting values: betapp (a number), betamarks (a matrix with one column per mark), marks_coefs_pp (one per mark), and log_tau and log_kappa (one per field, the point process field first, so of length 1 + sum(fields)).

Things to be aware of:

No missing marks. Every event needs a value for every mark. Removing events with missing marks also removes them from the point pattern, so the intensity will be underestimated; if many marks are missing, consider fitting the locations with fit_lgcp() using all events.
Gaussian and gamma marks have a fixed scale. stelfi does not estimate the standard deviation of Gaussian marks (or the scale of gamma marks); you supply its log through strfixed. A natural choice is the standard deviation of the marks, which is an upper bound for the residual standard deviation, and it is sensible to check that the conclusions do not change for smaller values (Section 7.4).
Binomial marks need the number of trials. For a yes/no mark (e.g., fatal or not) the marks are 0/1 and the number of trials is 1, which is the default (strfixed is a matrix of 1s).
Poisson marks are counts and the Poisson distribution assumes the variance equals the mean. Counts with occasional very large values (e.g., the number killed in an attack) are usually much more variable than this, and a binary or transformed mark may be more appropriate.
Marks are modelled at the mesh nodes and interpolated to the events, so the mesh (Chapter 5) affects the marks as well as the point process.

title: 7  Marked log-Gaussian Cox process
text:
7.2 A simulated example
Data were simulated from a marked LGCP with a single Gaussian mark within a 3 by 3 square. The point process has intercept \(\beta_{pp} = 4\) and a field with range \(r_{pp} = 1.5\) and standard deviation \(\sigma_{pp} = 1\). The mark has intercept \(\beta_m = 1\), link \(\alpha = 0.5\) (so marks are larger where events are more common), its own field with range \(r_m = 1.5\) and standard deviation \(\sigma_m = 0.5\), and a residual standard deviation of 0.3. The simulation has three steps:

Fields. Two independent random fields, \(G_{pp}(s)\) and \(G_m(s)\), are simulated at the nodes of a mesh using sim_lgcp() (only the simulated field, $x, is used). sim_lgcp() takes the field parameters on the internal scale, so the range and standard deviation are first converted to \(\kappa = \sqrt{8}/r\) and \(\tau = 1/(\sigma\sqrt{4\pi}\kappa)\) by the function spde_pars().
Events. The events are simulated by thinning: candidate events are simulated uniformly over the square at the maximum of the intensity \(\lambda_{\max}\), and each candidate at location \(s\) is kept with probability \(\lambda(s)/\lambda_{\max}\), where \(\log \lambda(s) = \beta_{pp} + G_{pp}(s)\) and the field at \(s\) is interpolated from the mesh nodes using fmesher::fm_basis().
Marks. The mark of each event is drawn from a normal distribution with mean \(\eta(s) = \beta_m + \alpha \log \lambda(s) + G_m(s)\) and standard deviation 0.3.


loc.d <- 3 * cbind(c(0, 1, 1, 0, 0), c(0, 0, 1, 1, 0))
domain <- sf::st_sf(geometry = sf::st_sfc(sf::st_polygon(list(loc.d))))
smesh <- fmesher::fm_mesh_2d(loc.domain = loc.d, offset = c(0.3, 1),
                             max.edge = c(0.3, 0.7), cutoff = 0.05)
truth <- c(betapp = 4, range_pp = 1.5, sigma_pp = 1,
           betam = 1, range_m = 1.5, sigma_m = 0.5, alpha = 0.5, sd_m = 0.3)
spde_pars <- function(range, sigma) {
    kappa <- unname(sqrt(8) / range); sigma <- unname(sigma)
    c(log_tau = log(1 / (sigma * sqrt(4 * pi) * kappa)), log_kappa = log(kappa))
}
set.seed(1)
## 1. the fields at the mesh nodes
g_pp <- as.vector(sim_lgcp(c(beta = 0, spde_pars(truth["range_pp"], truth["sigma_pp"])),
                           sf = domain, smesh = smesh)$x)
g_m <- as.vector(sim_lgcp(c(beta = 0, spde_pars(truth["range_m"], truth["sigma_m"])),
                          sf = domain, smesh = smesh)$x)
## 2. the events, by thinning
lmax <- exp(truth["betapp"] + max(g_pp))
n0 <- rpois(1, lmax * 9) ## candidates over the 3 by 3 square
cand <- data.frame(x = runif(n0, 0, 3), y = runif(n0, 0, 3))
A <- fmesher::fm_basis(smesh, loc = as.matrix(cand))
log_lambda <- truth["betapp"] + as.vector(A %*% g_pp)
keep <- runif(n0) < exp(log_lambda) / lmax
sim <- cand[keep, ]
## 3. the marks
eta <- truth["betam"] + truth["alpha"] * log_lambda[keep] + as.vector(A[keep, ] %*% g_m)
sim$m <- rnorm(nrow(sim), mean = eta, sd = truth["sd_m"])
rownames(sim) <- NULL

7.2.1 Fitting the model using stelfi
The mesh used to simulate the data is also used to fit the model, and the locations and marks are put into matrices. In practice the residual standard deviation of the marks is unknown, so, as suggested in Section 7.1.1, the standard deviation of the Gaussian mark is fixed at the standard deviation of the marks (through strfixed, on the log scale). The mark is given its own random field (fields = 1), so there are two fields: one for the point process and one for the mark.

marks <- cbind(m = sim$m)

fit <- fit_mlgcp(locs = locs, marks = marks, sf = domain, smesh = smesh,
                 parameters = parameters, methods = 0, fields = 1, strfixed = strfixed)

inlabru (Bachl et al. (2019)) can fit joint models with several likelihoods that share components. Below, the point process is an LGCP ("cp") with its own intercept and field, and the mark is Gaussian with its own intercept, its own field, and a scaled copy of the point process field (copy = "field_pp", the scaling being estimated). In stelfi the link \(\alpha\) multiplies the whole log intensity, \(\beta_{pp} + G_{pp}(s)\), whereas in inlabru the scaling multiplies only the field \(G_{pp}(s)\). The two models are the same, but the mark intercepts differ by \(\alpha \beta_{pp}\), so the table shows \(\beta_m + \alpha \beta_{pp}\) for stelfi and for the truth (\(1 + 0.5 \times 4 = 3\)). The two packages agree closely with each other, and with the truth, on the point process intercept and the mark intercept, and both correctly find that the marks are larger where events are more common (a positive link), although both overestimate the link. As in Section 6.2, the range and standard deviation of the fields are harder to pin down from a single dataset. Note in particular that both packages underestimate the standard deviation of the mark’s own field, \(\sigma_m\). This is a consequence of fixing the residual standard deviation at the standard deviation of the marks (0.745), which is much larger than the true value (0.3): the model then attributes some of the spatial variation in the marks to residual noise rather than to the field. This is why it is worth refitting with a smaller fixed standard deviation (see Section 7.4).

section: 7.3 An applied example: fatal terrorism attacks in Iraq
text:
7.3 An applied example: fatal terrorism attacks in Iraq
In Section 6.3.2 the locations of terrorism events in Iraq were modelled. The iraq_terrorism data also record the number of people killed in each attack (nkill). Here a marked LGCP is used to ask whether the probability that an attack is fatal varies over space, and whether attacks are more or less likely to be fatal where attacks are more frequent. The mark is binary: 1 if at least one person was killed and 0 otherwise.

7.3.1 Preparing the data
The number killed is missing for some events. These events are removed (see Section 7.1.1 for the consequences). The locations are projected to km and the boundary of Iraq obtained exactly as in Section 6.3.2.

data("iraq_terrorism", package = "stelfi")
sum(is.na(iraq_terrorism$nkill)) ## events with a missing number killed

[1] 396

iraq <- iraq_terrorism[!is.na(iraq_terrorism$nkill), ]
locs_km <- sf::st_coordinates(sf::st_transform(iraq, crs = 32638)) / 1000
colnames(locs_km) <- c("x", "y")
marks_iraq <- cbind(fatal = as.numeric(iraq$nkill > 0))
table(marks_iraq)

marks_iraq
   0    1 
 854 2958 

iraq_sf <- rnaturalearth::ne_countries(country = "Iraq", scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf") |>
    sf::st_transform(crs = 32638) |>
    sf::st_union()
iraq_sf_km <- sf::st_sf(geometry = sf::st_geometry(iraq_sf) / 1000)
sf::st_crs(iraq_sf_km) <- NA

A mesh slightly coarser than the adequate mesh of Sensitivity to the mesh in Section 6.3.2 (max.edge = c(60, 200), cutoff = 15) is used, to keep the fit quick. The mark is binomial (methods = 2) with one trial per event (the default strfixed), and has its own random field.

                                  max.edge = c(60, 200), cutoff = 15)

parameters_iraq <- list(betapp = log(nrow(locs_km) / area_km2),
                        betamarks = matrix(0, nrow = 1, ncol = 1), marks_coefs_pp = 0,
                        log_tau = c(0, 0), log_kappa = log(c(sqrt(8) / 50, sqrt(8) / 50)))
fit_iraq <- fit_mlgcp(locs = locs_km, marks = marks_iraq, sf = iraq_sf_km, smesh = smesh_iraq,

coefs <- get_coefs(fit_iraq)

title: 7  Marked log-Gaussian Cox process
text:
7.4 Goodness-of-fit
A marked LGCP has two parts, and each should be checked:

the point process. The locations are modelled exactly as in an LGCP, so the simulation envelopes of Section 6.4 can be used; and
the marks. The fitted model gives a predicted value of each mark (e.g., the probability that each attack is fatal) which can be compared with the observed marks.

To check the marks, the fitted linear predictor \(\eta_j(s)\) is needed at each event. The function below calculates it from the fitted model (for models without covariates), following the definition of \(\eta_j(s)\) above.

mark_predictor <- function(fit, smesh, locs, mark = 1) {
    pars <- fit$env$parList(par = fit$env$last.par.best) ## estimates, including the fields
    fields <- fit$env$data$mark_field
    log_lambda <- pars$betapp[1] + pars$x[, 1] ## log intensity of the point process at each node
    eta <- pars$betamarks[1, mark] + pars$marks_coefs_pp[mark] * log_lambda
    if (fields[mark] == 1) eta <- eta + pars$x[, 1 + cumsum(fields)[mark]] ## the mark's own field
    as.vector(fmesher::fm_basis(smesh, loc = locs) %*% eta) ## interpolate to the events
}


7.4.1 The simulated example
For the Gaussian mark the linear predictor is the predicted mean, so the residuals are the observed minus the predicted marks. If the model is adequate the residuals should show no pattern against the predicted values, and their standard deviation should be no larger than the fixed standard deviation used in strfixed.

pred <- mark_predictor(fit, smesh, locs)
res <- sim$m - pred
c(residual_sd = sd(res), fixed_sd = sd(sim$m), true_sd = unname(truth["sd_m"]))

residual_sd    fixed_sd     true_sd 
  0.3406189   0.7447414   0.3000000 

patchwork::wrap_plots(
    ggplot(data.frame(pred, res), aes(x = pred, y = res)) + geom_point() +
        geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") + theme_minimal() +
        xlab("Predicted mark") + ylab("Residual"),
    ggplot(data.frame(res), aes(sample = res)) + stat_qq() + stat_qq_line() +
        theme_minimal() + ggtitle("Normal QQ plot of residuals"),
    nrow = 1)








The residuals show no obvious pattern and look roughly normal. Their standard deviation is much smaller than the fixed standard deviation, because the random fields explain much of the variation in the marks, and it is close to the true value. Since the standard deviation is fixed rather than estimated, it is worth refitting with strfixed set to the log of the residual standard deviation and checking that the conclusions do not change.

strfixed_res <- matrix(log(sd(res)), nrow = nrow(locs), ncol = 1)
fit_res <- fit_mlgcp(locs = locs, marks = marks, sf = domain, smesh = smesh,
                     parameters = parameters, methods = 0, fields = 1, strfixed = strfixed_res)
coefs_res <- get_coefs(fit_res)
kappa_res <- coefs_res[rownames(coefs_res) == "kappa", 1]
tau_res <- coefs_res[rownames(coefs_res) == "tau", 1]
rbind(original = c(link = stelfi["marks_coefs_pp", 1], sigma_m = st_sd[2]),
      refitted = c(link = coefs_res["marks_coefs_pp", 1],
                   sigma_m = 1 / sqrt(4 * pi * kappa_res[2]^2 * tau_res[2]^2)),
      truth = c(link = unname(truth["alpha"]), sigma_m = unname(truth["sigma_m"])))

              link sigma_m.kappa
original 0.5851238     0.2156919
refitted 0.5901986     0.2941287
truth    0.5000000     0.5000000


The link is essentially unchanged, but the estimated standard deviation of the mark’s field increases towards the true value: with less of the variation in the marks attributed to noise, more is attributed to the field.


7.4.2 The applied example
For a binary mark the linear predictor is on the logit scale, so the predicted probability that an attack is fatal is \(\text{logit}^{-1}(\eta)\). A simple check of these predictions is to group the attacks by their predicted probability (here into ten groups of equal size) and compare the average predicted probability in each group with the observed proportion of fatal attacks. For a well calibrated model the points should lie close to the line \(y = x\).

p_fatal <- plogis(mark_predictor(fit_iraq, smesh_iraq, locs_km))
group <- cut(p_fatal, breaks = unique(quantile(p_fatal, probs = seq(0, 1, 0.1))),
             include.lowest = TRUE)
calib <- data.frame(predicted = tapply(p_fatal, group, mean),
                    observed = tapply(marks_iraq[, 1], group, mean),
                    n = as.vector(table(group)))
calib$se <- sqrt(calib$observed * (1 - calib$observed) / calib$n)
ggplot(calib, aes(x = predicted, y = observed)) +
    geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = observed - 2 * se, ymax = observed + 2 * se)) +
    theme_minimal() + xlab("Predicted probability fatal") + ylab("Observed proportion fatal")








Points (with approximate 95% intervals) close to the dashed line indicate that the predicted probabilities are consistent with what was observed. Note that this is a fairly weak check, since the same data were used to fit the model; a more stringent check is to fit the model to part of the data (e.g., some years) and compare the predictions with the rest. The point process part of the model should also be checked using simulation envelopes (Section 6.4).




Bachl, Fabian E., Finn Lindgren, David L. Borchers, and Janine B. Illian. 2019. “inlabru: An R Package for Bayesian Spatial Modelling from Ecological Survey Data.” Methods in Ecology and Evolution 10: 760–66. https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13168.

title: 8  Spatiotemporal self-exciting models
text:
8.1 The model and your data
A spatiotemporal self-exciting model combines ideas from the Hawkes process (Chapter 2) and the LGCP (Chapter 6). Events have a time and a location, and each event temporarily increases the chance of further events nearby, in both time and space. Earthquake aftershocks, the spread of crime (“near repeat” burglaries), and outbreaks of disease are typical examples. The intensity used by stelfi (see Reinhart (2018)) is
\[\lambda(s,t) = \mu + \alpha \sum_{i:\tau_i<t} \text{exp}(-\beta (t-\tau_i))\, f(s - x_i), \tag{8.1}\]
where \(\tau_i\) and \(x_i\) are the time and location of event \(i\), and
Two extensions are available:
get_coefs() reports mu and coefs (the log of the background rate, followed by any covariate coefficients), alpha, beta, xsigma, ysigma, rho, and, with GMRF = TRUE, the field parameters kappa and tau.

title: 8  Spatiotemporal self-exciting models
text:
\(\mu\) is the background rate, the expected number of spontaneous events per unit area per unit time;
\(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) describe the temporal self-excitement, exactly as for a Hawkes process: each event triggers on average \(\alpha/\beta\) further events (if all of its spatial influence falls within the study region), and its influence decays with time scale \(1/\beta\); and
\(f(\cdot)\) is the spatial triggering kernel, a bivariate normal density centred on the triggering event with standard deviations \(\sigma_x\) and \(\sigma_y\) (in the x and y directions) and correlation \(\rho\). So triggered events tend to occur within a couple of standard deviations of the event that triggered them, and \(\rho \neq 0\) means triggering is stronger along one diagonal direction than the other.



A spatially varying background. Setting GMRF = TRUE replaces \(\mu\) with \(\mu(s) = \text{exp}(\beta_0 + G(s))\), where \(G(s)\) is a Gaussian random field as in an LGCP. Spatial covariates can also be included in the background via the covariates argument (one row per mesh node). This is important if some areas simply have more events than others, as otherwise this will be mistaken for self-excitement.
A spreading kernel. Setting time_independent = FALSE makes the spread of the kernel grow with time since the triggering event (its covariance is proportional to \(t - \tau_i\)), appropriate when the triggering mechanism travels at a finite speed. This is very memory intensive.



8.1.1 What your data need to look like
fit_stelfi() needs

times, a numeric vector of event times, sorted with no ties (exactly as for a Hawkes process, Section 2.1.1);
locs, a data frame with columns x and y giving the location of each event, in the same order as times;
sf, an sf polygon of the study region; and
smesh, a mesh of the study region (Chapter 5).

Things to be aware of:

Use projected coordinates in sensible units (e.g., km), as for an LGCP (Section 6.1.1). The units of time and distance set the units of the parameters: \(\mu\) is then events per km\(^2\) per day (say) and \(\sigma_x\), \(\sigma_y\) are in km.
The mesh is used to integrate the intensity over the study region, both the background and the spatial kernel of every event. The mesh therefore needs to be fine relative to the spread of the kernel (\(\sigma_x\), \(\sigma_y\)) where there are events, otherwise the integral of the kernel is inaccurate and so are the estimates. A good approach is to build the mesh around the events (loc = locs) with a small cutoff, which gives small triangles where events are and larger ones elsewhere. fit_stelfi() gives a warning if the mesh looks too coarse for the estimated kernel, and the accuracy can be checked in more detail after fitting (Section 8.4).
Edge effects. Events near the edge of the study region trigger events that may fall outside it, and are therefore unobserved. The model accounts for this (the integral of the kernel only covers the study region), but the study region should be the region where events could have been observed.
Computation. The likelihood involves every pair of events, so the cost grows with the square of the number of events. A few hundred to a few thousand events is feasible; for more, consider a subset (e.g., a time window or the larger events).
Starting values. parameters is a list with coefs (the log of the background rate, or alternatively mu, the background rate itself; if neither is given a crude default is used), alpha, beta, xsigma, ysigma, rho, and, with GMRF = TRUE, kappa and tau. Choose xsigma and ysigma to be roughly the distance over which you expect triggering to occur, and \(\alpha < \beta\). The model can be sensitive to starting values, particularly with GMRF = TRUE, so it is worth trying a few.

title: 8  Spatiotemporal self-exciting models
text:
8.2 A simulated example
Data were simulated from Equation 8.1 within the (elliptical) study region of the xyt dataset (see Chapter 10), with background rate \(\mu = 1\), \(\alpha = 2\) and \(\beta = 4\) (so each event triggers on average \(2/4 = 0.5\) events), and a kernel with \(\sigma_x = 0.5\), \(\sigma_y = 0.25\) and \(\rho = 0\) (so triggering spreads twice as far in the x direction as in the y direction).
stelfi does not have a separate simulation function for this model. Instead, the fitted model object returned by fit_stelfi() has a simulate() method that simulates a new point pattern, over the same study region and time period, from the model with any given parameter values. So below the model is first fitted to the xyt data (the estimates themselves are not used), and the simulate() method is then called with the true parameter values. These must be given on the scale used internally by stelfi: the log of \(\mu\) (coefs), the logit of \(\alpha/\beta\), the logs of \(\beta\), \(\sigma_x\) and \(\sigma_y\), and \(\text{atanh}(\rho)\).

data(xyt, package = "stelfi")
domain <- sf::st_as_sf(xyt$window)
bnd <- fmesher::fm_as_segm(as.matrix(sf::st_coordinates(domain)[, 1:2]))
smesh <- fmesher::fm_mesh_2d(boundary = bnd, max.edge = 0.75, cutoff = 0.3)
fit0 <- fit_stelfi(times = xyt$t, locs = data.frame(x = xyt$x, y = xyt$y), sf = domain,
                   smesh = smesh, parameters = list(alpha = 1, beta = 3, xsigma = 0.3,
                                                    ysigma = 0.3, rho = 0))
truth <- c(mu = 1, alpha = 2, beta = 4, xsigma = 0.5, ysigma = 0.25, rho = 0)
set.seed(2)
sim <- fit0$simulate(par = c(coefs = log(1), logit_abratio = qlogis(2 / 4), log_beta = log(4),
                             log_xsigma = log(0.5), log_ysigma = log(0.25), atanh_rho = 0))
## sort the events by time
ord <- order(sim$times)
locs <- data.frame(x = sim$locs[ord, 1], y = sim$locs[ord, 2])
times <- sim$times[ord]

title: 8  Spatiotemporal self-exciting models
text:
8.3 An applied example: Canterbury earthquakes
The Canterbury earthquakes were modelled in time only in Section 3.3 and Section 4.3. Here their locations are included. To keep computation manageable, only the 379 earthquakes of magnitude 4 and above are used.

8.3.1 Preparing the data
The earthquakes are projected to New Zealand Transverse Mercator (EPSG:2193) and converted to km. Times are in days since the first earthquake, jittered to remove ties (Section 3.3), and the data are sorted by time.

data(nz_earthquakes, package = "stelfi")
eq <- nz_earthquakes[nz_earthquakes$magnitude >= 4, ]
xy <- sf::st_coordinates(sf::st_transform(eq, crs = 2193)) / 1000
set.seed(1)
days <- as.numeric(difftime(eq$origintime, min(eq$origintime), units = "days")) +
    runif(nrow(eq), 0, 1 / (24 * 60))
ord <- order(days)
times <- days[ord] - min(days)
locs <- data.frame(x = xy[ord, 1], y = xy[ord, 2])

The catalogue does not come with a study region, so here the region is taken to be the convex hull of the earthquakes, extended by 20 km. In your own application the study region should reflect where events could have been recorded.

domain <- sf::st_as_sf(locs, coords = c("x", "y")) |>
    sf::st_union() |>
    sf::st_convex_hull() |>
    sf::st_buffer(20)
domain <- sf::st_sf(geometry = domain)

The mesh is built around the earthquakes with a small cutoff (1 km), so that triangles are small where earthquakes are (much smaller than the few km over which aftershocks are expected) and larger elsewhere.

smesh <- fmesher::fm_mesh_2d(loc = locs, boundary = fmesher::fm_as_segm(domain),
                             max.edge = c(30, 100), cutoff = 1)
smesh$n

    geom_sf(data = mesh_2_sf(smesh), fill = NA, linewidth = 0.2) +

title: 8  Spatiotemporal self-exciting models
text:
8.4 Goodness-of-fit

8.4.1 Checking the mesh
stelfi integrates the spatial kernel of each event over the study region using the mesh. For an event well inside the region the integral should be close to 1 (and less than 1 for an event near the edge). This can be checked by comparing the mesh-based integral with an accurate Monte Carlo estimate (the proportion of points simulated from the kernel that fall inside the study region).

kernel_volume <- function(pars, locs, sf, smesh, n_mc = 2000) {
    sigma <- matrix(c(pars["xsigma", 1]^2,
                      rep(pars["rho", 1] * pars["xsigma", 1] * pars["ysigma", 1], 2),
                      pars["ysigma", 1]^2), ncol = 2)
    w <- get_weights(smesh, sf)$weights
    window <- spatstat.geom::as.owin(sf)
    t(sapply(seq_len(nrow(locs)), function(i) {
        centre <- unlist(locs[i, c("x", "y")])
        mesh <- sum(w * mvtnorm::dmvnorm(smesh$loc[, 1:2], mean = centre, sigma = sigma))
        draws <- mvtnorm::rmvnorm(n_mc, mean = centre, sigma = sigma)
        mc <- mean(spatstat.geom::inside.owin(draws[, 1], draws[, 2], window))
        c(mesh = mesh, monte_carlo = mc)
    }))
}
set.seed(1)
vol <- kernel_volume(pars_eq, locs, domain, smesh)
summary(vol)

For 77% of the earthquakes the mesh-based integral is within 0.1 of the Monte Carlo value. Where they differ a lot (typically isolated earthquakes in parts of the region where the mesh is coarse) the mesh should be refined.


8.4.2 Checking the temporal pattern
Integrating Equation 8.1 over the study region gives the intensity of the event times, which is a marked Hawkes process (Chapter 3) with background rate \(\int \mu(s) ds\) (the background integrated over the region) and with the mark of each event being the integral of its kernel over the study region (the Monte Carlo values above). The goodness-of-fit checks of Section 2.4 can therefore be applied to the times, using show_hawkes_GOF() with a list containing the times, the parameters, and the marks.

w <- get_weights(smesh, domain)$weights
mu_total <- sum(w * exp(pars_eq["coefs", 1] + as.vector(get_fields(fit_eq_gmrf, smesh))))
temporal <- list(times = times, marks = vol[, "monte_carlo"],
                 params = c(mu = mu_total, alpha = pars_eq["alpha", 1], beta = pars_eq["beta", 1]))


show_hawkes_GOF(temporal)

data:  interarrivals

As for the purely temporal models of the earthquakes (Section 3.4), the tests reject the model and the plots show the same features: the exponential decay in time cannot describe both the burst of activity immediately after a large earthquake and the long tail of aftershocks that follows, and every earthquake is assumed to trigger equally regardless of its magnitude. Adding space improves the description of where aftershocks occur, but does not fix these temporal limitations.

title: 9  Simple RTMB templates
text:
9.1 A marked Hawkes process
stelfi fits its models using likelihoods written in C++ for TMB (Kristensen et al. (2016)). The RTMB package (Kristensen (2024)) lets you write the same kind of likelihood in R, while still getting automatic differentiation (fast and accurate gradients) and the Laplace approximation for random effects. This chapter gives simple RTMB versions of two of the stelfi likelihoods, a marked Hawkes process and a spatial LGCP, and checks that they give the same answers as stelfi. They are intended as a starting point if you want to see exactly what is being fitted or want to modify a model, for example to use a different self-excitement kernel, add covariates in a different way, or change a distribution.
Every RTMB model follows the same pattern:
See the RTMB introduction for more details.
The function below is the negative log-likelihood of the marked Hawkes process of Equation 3.1 (an unmarked process is obtained by setting all marks to 1). For a Hawkes process with intensity \(\lambda(t)\) observed over \([0, T]\) the log-likelihood is
\[\log L = \sum_{i=1}^n \log \lambda(\tau_i) - \int_0^T \lambda(t) dt.\]
The sum over past events in \(\lambda(\tau_i)\) is computed recursively (the term A below), which makes the likelihood fast to evaluate. The parameters are transformed so that they can take any value during optimisation: \(\mu\) and \(\beta\) are on the log scale, and \(\alpha\) is parameterised through the logit of the average branching ratio, which keeps \(\alpha \bar{m} < \beta\) (Chapter 3). As in stelfi, the integral is taken up to the last event.
marked_hawkes_nll <- function(params) {
    getAll(data, params)
    mu <- exp(log_mu)
    beta <- exp(log_beta)
    alpha <- plogis(logit_abratio) * beta / mean(marks)
    n <- length(times)
    ## A[i] = sum over j < i of marks[j] * exp(-beta * (times[i] - times[j]))
    A <- advector(numeric(n))
    for (i in 2:n) {
        A[i] <- exp(-beta * (times[i] - times[i - 1])) * (marks[i - 1] + A[i - 1])
    }
    ## sum of log intensities at the events
    loglik <- sum(log(mu + alpha * A))
    ## minus the integral of the intensity from 0 to the last event
    loglik <- loglik - mu * times[n] - (alpha / beta) * (sum(marks) - marks[n] - A[n])
    ADREPORT(mu)
    ADREPORT(alpha)
    ADREPORT(beta)
    -loglik
}
This is applied to the Canterbury earthquakes with marks \(\text{exp}(\text{magnitude} - 3)\), prepared exactly as in Section 3.3.
data(nz_earthquakes, package = "stelfi")
eq <- data.frame(time = nz_earthquakes$origintime, magnitude = nz_earthquakes$magnitude)
eq$days <- as.numeric(difftime(eq$time, min(eq$time), units = "days"))
set.seed(1)
eq$days <- eq$days + runif(nrow(eq), 0, 1 / (24 * 60))
eq <- eq[order(eq$days), ]
eq$days <- eq$days - eq$days[1]
eq$mark <- exp(eq$magnitude - 3)
data <- list(times = eq$days, marks = eq$mark)
params <- list(log_mu = log(0.3), logit_abratio = 0, log_beta = log(2))
obj <- MakeADFun(marked_hawkes_nll, params, silent = TRUE)
opt <- nlminb(obj$par, obj$fn, obj$gr)
summary(sdreport(obj), "report")

       Estimate Std. Error
mu    0.3166995 0.01831556
alpha 1.5253057 0.09100412
beta  3.1914302 0.19620356
The same model fitted using stelfi:
fit <- fit_hawkes(times = eq$days, parameters = c(mu = 0.3, alpha = 1, beta = 2), marks = eq$mark)
get_coefs(fit)

       Estimate Std. Error
mu    0.3165789 0.01831468
alpha 1.5257779 0.09103272
beta  3.1923044 0.19626381
The estimates agree (up to small differences due to the optimiser).
Some ideas for modifying the template: replace the exponential kernel with another kernel (you will need its integral, and for most kernels the recursive calculation of A no longer works, so the sum has to be over all pairs of events, which is slower); let the background vary with time (as in Section 2.5); or let the effect of the mark be estimated, e.g., using marks^gamma with \(\gamma\) an additional parameter.

title: 9  Simple RTMB templates
text:
9.2 A spatial LGCP
Given events \(s_1, ..., s_n\) in a study region \(D\), the log-likelihood of a Poisson process with intensity \(\lambda(s) = \text{exp}(\beta_0 + G(s))\), conditional on the random field, is
\[\log L = \sum_{j=1}^n \log \lambda(s_j) - \int_D \lambda(s)\,ds.\]
The field is represented on the mesh (Chapter 5) as \(G(s) = \sum_i \psi_i(s) x_i\), where the \(\psi_i\) are piecewise linear basis functions and the values at the mesh nodes \(\boldsymbol{x}\) have a multivariate normal distribution with mean zero and sparse precision matrix
\[\boldsymbol{Q} = \tau^2(\kappa^4 \boldsymbol{C} + 2\kappa^2 \boldsymbol{G} + \boldsymbol{G}\boldsymbol{C}^{-1}\boldsymbol{G}),\]
where \(\boldsymbol{C}\) and \(\boldsymbol{G}\) are matrices that depend only on the mesh (returned by fmesher::fm_fem()). Two more ingredients are needed:

a sparse “projection” matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\) that gives the value of the field at any set of locations from the values at the mesh nodes, i.e., \(G(s_j) = (\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x})_j\) (from fmesher::fm_basis()); and
integration points \(u_k\) with weights \(w_k\) (from fmesher::fm_int()), so that the integral over the study region is approximated by \(\int_D \lambda(s)ds \approx \sum_k w_k \lambda(u_k)\). The weights sum to the area of \(D\).

The random field \(\boldsymbol{x}\) is a random effect: it is integrated out of the likelihood using the Laplace approximation by naming it in the random argument of MakeADFun().
The sasquatch data are used, prepared exactly as in Section 6.3.1.

data("sasquatch", package = "stelfi")
sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)
us <- maps::map("usa", fill = TRUE, plot = FALSE) |>
    sf::st_as_sf() |>
    sf::st_make_valid() |>
    sf::st_transform(crs = 5070)
us_km <- sf::st_sf(geometry = sf::st_union(sf::st_geometry(us)) / 1000)
sf::st_crs(us_km) <- NA ## planar km, matching the mesh
locs <- sf::st_transform(sasquatch, crs = 5070) |>
    sf::st_coordinates() |>
    as.data.frame()
names(locs) <- c("x", "y")
locs <- locs / 1000
smesh <- fmesher::fm_mesh_2d(loc = locs[, 1:2], max.edge = c(200, 500), cutoff = 100)

The data needed by the template are the three mesh matrices, the projection matrices for the events and for the integration points, and the integration weights.

fem <- fmesher::fm_fem(smesh, order = 2)
as_T <- function(M) as(as(M, "generalMatrix"), "TsparseMatrix") ## sparse format used by RTMB
ips <- fmesher::fm_int(smesh, samplers = us_km)
data <- list(C = as_T(fem$c0), G1 = as_T(fem$g1), G2 = as_T(fem$g2),
             A_pts = fmesher::fm_basis(smesh, loc = as.matrix(locs)),
             A_ips = fmesher::fm_basis(smesh, loc = sf::st_coordinates(ips)[, 1:2]),
             w = ips$weight)


lgcp_nll <- function(params) {
    getAll(data, params)
    tau <- exp(log_tau)
    kappa <- exp(log_kappa)
    ## precision matrix of the field at the mesh nodes
    Q <- tau^2 * (kappa^4 * C + 2 * kappa^2 * G1 + G2)
    ## the random field: a multivariate normal with precision Q
    nll <- -dgmrf(x, 0, Q, log = TRUE)
    ## log intensity at the events and at the integration points
    eta_pts <- beta + A_pts %*% x
    eta_ips <- beta + A_ips %*% x
    ## minus (sum of log intensity at events - integral of the intensity)
    nll <- nll - sum(eta_pts) + sum(w * exp(eta_ips))
    ## range and standard deviation of the field
    range <- sqrt(8) / kappa
    stdev <- 1 / sqrt(4 * pi * kappa^2 * tau^2)
    ADREPORT(beta)
    ADREPORT(range)
    ADREPORT(stdev)
    nll
}


params <- list(beta = log(nrow(locs) / sum(data$w)), log_tau = log(1),
               log_kappa = log(1), x = rep(0, smesh$n))
obj <- MakeADFun(lgcp_nll, params, random = "x", silent = TRUE)
opt <- nlminb(obj$par, obj$fn, obj$gr)
sdr <- sdreport(obj)
summary(sdr, "report")

         Estimate  Std. Error
beta    -9.877046   0.4959888
range 1155.765168 244.2988155
stdev    1.426333   0.2419242


The same model fitted using stelfi:

fit <- fit_lgcp(locs = locs, sf = us_km, smesh = smesh,
                parameters = c(beta = log(nrow(locs) / sum(data$w)), log_tau = log(1), log_kappa = log(1)))
get_coefs(fit)[c("beta", "range", "stdev"), ]

        Estimate  Std. Error
beta   -9.937127   0.3865464
range 813.993038 147.9889397
stdev   1.419026   0.1880638


The estimates are close, but not identical, because the two implementations approximate the likelihood slightly differently: stelfi counts the events closest to each mesh node and gives each node the area of the study region closest to it, whereas the template uses the exact event locations and integration points. The estimated field (the values of the random effects at the optimum) can be extracted from the sdreport() and plotted as before.

x_hat <- as.list(sdr, "Estimate")$x
show_field(x_hat, smesh = smesh, sf = us_km, clip = TRUE) + theme_void()








Some ideas for modifying the template:

covariates: replace beta with a vector of coefficients and the intercept in eta_pts and eta_ips with a design matrix times that vector (e.g., X_pts %*% beta), with the covariates evaluated at the events and at the integration points;
sampling effort: add the log of a known effort surface (evaluated at the events and integration points) to eta_pts and eta_ips as an offset; and
marks: add the log-likelihood of each mark, with a linear predictor that includes the field at the events (A_pts %*% x), to give a marked LGCP (Chapter 7).

10.3 Simulated data

xyt
A simulated self-exciting spatiotemporal point pattern of 653 events, stored as a stppp object (from the stpp package): the locations are xyt$x and xyt$y, the times are xyt$t (in \([0, 2]\)), and the study region is xyt$window (a spatstat owin, which can be converted to sf using sf::st_as_sf(xyt$window)). Its study region is used in Section 8.2.

data(xyt, package = "stelfi")
ggplot(data.frame(x = xyt$x, y = xyt$y, t = xyt$t), aes(x = x, y = y, size = t)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
    geom_sf(data = sf::st_as_sf(xyt$window), fill = NA, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
    theme_void()










marked
